## S: spank–System

### spank

 
<i>verb</i>. to milk cows

[NOTES: Usually in the phrase "spank cows"]

>  <b>SCOTT</b> We got on pretty well and spanked, that is milked, his cows for him night and morning. <i>(1897,How I Stole 10,000 Sheep,8</i>)

>  <b>BALLANTYNE</b> They spanked cows. <i>(1948,Cunninghams, The,199</i>)

>  <b>SMITH</b> The dairy farmer.. has to spank cows before breakfast and he has to spank them again before his tea. <i>(1949,From N to Z,106</i>)

>  "Going to spank cows?" was usually the incredulous comment. <i>(Sep 1971,NZ Dairy Exporter,131</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>. [Rural] to milk cows.

>  <b>ANDERSON</b> We took it in turn, day by day, to cook the meals, wash up, kill a sheep and spank the cow very occasionally. <i>(1962,Life's Roundabout, A,45</i>)

>  'Going to spank cows?' was usually the incredulous comment. <i>(Sep 1971,NZ Dairy Exporter,131</i>)

### SPANZ

 
<i>abbreviation</i>. South Pacific Airlines of New Zealand

>  Spanz Viewmaster DC3s trundled through New Zealand skies until February 1966 and were a byword for service... The can-do airline was the brainchild of two NAC captains, Rex Daniell, of Auckland, and Bob Anderson, of Paraparaumu... In some rural centres the public service mindset appplied so that bowsers were locked at 5pm on the knocker - woe betide a Spanz DC3 that failed to beat the knock-off clock. <i>(Dec 6, 2000,Evening Post,23</i>)

<i>noun</i>.

>  "Our pilots and crew are friendly people" was a dictum of Spanzmanship. "The hostess, for instance, will offer you cigarettes, coffee and magazines." <i>(Dec 6, 2000,Evening Post,24</i>)

### spar

 
<i>noun</i>. a tree trunk; ?round timber distinct from baulks; ?spar =unsawn trunk ?log =sawn length (but confused)

See: -

>  <b>ELDER</b> I should wish you to bring as much hemp as you possibly can, and such spars and timber as you may, with Mr. Hall, judge valuable. Pork, if it is to be obtained, and salt fish, rosin, or any other natural productions. <i>(1934,Marsden's Lieutenants,55</i>) [NOTES: 1814 Marsden in Elder Marsden's Lieutenants (1934) 55]

>  <b>ELDER</b> After the vessel had landed our supplies, she went up to the timber ground to take in a cargo of spars, and I went up to her in my own boat manned with natives to assist and encourage the timber ground natives to cut the spars and tow them down the river convenient to the vessel. <i>(1934,Marsden's Lieutenants,220</i>) [NOTES: 1819 May 5 William Hall in Elder Marsden's Lieutenants (1934) 220]

>  <b>BISCOE</b> ... the Cutter's Bowsprit being sprung I went over ... to endeavour to procure a spar to make one. I found one 37 feet long for which I paid 36lbs. of Brazil Tobacco. <i>(Nov 4, 1831,Journal</i>) [NOTES: 1831 Nov 4 J.Biscoe Journal in 1913 McNab Old Whaling Days 416]

>  Boat in Pigeon Bay - cutting spars for house ... [Apr 16] 2 boats fetching Spars Flags &c. for a house, <i>(Apr 15, 1836,Piraki Log,33,Anson 1911</i>)

>  J.Murray The houses are built of spars cut from the forest <i>(1840,NZ Journal,24/302</i>)

>  They next attend to dragging the spar (tree) through the bush into the water; this consumes much time and labour; small round pieces of timber being laid down as `ways' for the spar to glide over. <i>(1840,Manners & Customs of the NZers,1/169</i>)

>  <b>WILKES</b> The Kaurie and Kaikotia pines yield spars which for large ships are not surpassed by any in the world. <i>(1852,U.S. Exploring Expedition,1/317</i>) [NOTES: 1840 Mar in 1852 Wilkes U.S. Exploring Expedition 1/317]

>  <b>BAINES</b> I first cut a trench in the rock right across the bed of the creek, into which I placed a squared spar. I did the same up the good or rock side of the stream. On the other bank I made a `wing' by driving piles [for a flood-dam]. <i>(1874,Edward Crewe,174</i>)

>  <b>MEREDITH</b> [round timber] The chimney [of the camp] is built of sods to a certain height, and finished off with a sheet of galvanised iron or round spars plastered with mud on the outside. <i>(1875,Adventuring in Maoriland in the Seventies,133,1935</i>)

>  <b>COWAN</b> This post, a <i>puriri</i> spar about 30 feet high, was named by the Maoris `Poututaki', ... <i>(1922,NZ Wars, The,1/145</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>.

>  <b>HARPER</b> The half-axes were necessary in case we had to cut a tree down to `spar' the river or a bad creek; the bill-hooks were for blazing a track. <i>(1896,Pioneer Work in the Alps of NZ,182</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>. lay a spar across

>  <b>HARPER</b> ... a small axe in case it was necessary to cut a tree for `sparring' a creek; ... <i>(1896,Pioneer Work in the Alps of NZ,215</i>)

### SPARC

 
<i>abbreviation</i>. Sport and Recreation New Zealand

>  Sport and Recreation New Zealand (Sparc) announced in June that it was scrapping the Community Sport Fund, a 30-year-old system that allowed councils to allocate sports funding to local clubs for development purposes... Community sports grants were for grassroots development, and now the council, community and sporting organisations were waiting to find out what Sparc was going to do with its money. <i>(Aug 19, 2002,Dominion Post,A9</i>)

>  SPARC (which another Wellington newspaper pointed out is CRAP with an S spelt backwards) also picked cycling, swimming and athletics as part of a (ahem) revitalisation strategy... <i>(Jun 26, 2002,Capital Times,18</i>)

>  The new sports and recreation quango, Sparc, could not have picked a better name. At present, Sparcs are flying throughout the country at the quango's unilateral decision to axe the Community Sports Fund (CSF). <i>(Aug 21, 2002,Capital Times,18</i>)

>  SPARC, the new funding agency for New Zealand Sport, swiftly upset most of those it is supposed to help in June when it rated 10 sports above all others in terms of priority. <i>(Sep 4, 2002,Dominion Post,D9</i>)

>  "In a cricketing context.. Sparc is 27-8 after 45 overs. They need to get some runs on the board and they need them soon." <i>(Mar 15, 2003,Listener (New Zealand Listener),37</i>)

>  Unfortunately [obtaining resources] relies on Sparc, the only wicked fiary in this otherwise unreal fairytale. <i>(Sep 4, 2002,Capital Times,22</i>)

>  Hill said that about half of the Sports Foundation and Hillary Commission staff had been retained by Sparc... Sparc axed the Community Sports Funding scheme which had served the grass roots since 1973, to howls of outrage from councils and sports bodies. <i>(Mar 26, 2003,Dominion Post,D3</i>)

<i>verb</i>. to become merry, excited (with liquor)

### sparkie

 
<i>noun</i>. electrician

### sparrow-fart

 
<i>noun</i>. daybreak

>  <b>IRELAND</b> 'Get it down quick,' he would whisper so as not to wake the whole household. 'We'll have a boatload of fish before sparrow-fart.' <i>(1998,Under the Bridge & Over the Moon,119</i>)

>  We were fazed for a minute as the handle "lovely gent" didn't seem to fit anyone we know [sic], but we fought back gamely by claiming that "this bloody Skypoo was planning to shoot through at sparrow fart tomorrow without paying you his tariff," and a fascinating screaming match developed between the descendant of the old Phonecians and her with the gasper and pom-pommed slippers. <i>(Nov 1986,Geological Society of NZ Newsletter,74/78</i>)

>  <b>MITCHELL</b> <i>sparrow fart</i>: Time so early in the morning no English immigrant has ever heard this mysterious noise. All New Zealanders hear it; indeed the sound of their housework probably disturbs the sparrow in the first place. <i>(1972,Half-Gallon Quarter-Acre Pavlova Paradise, The,183</i>)

>  <b>HILLIARD</b> [Maori woman speaks] `... I'll have to get up at sparrow-te tomorrow ...' `Sparrow <i>what</i>?' `Sparrow-te,' she said decisively. `Sparrow-fart is the expression.' `I know ... You've got your way of saying it. I've got mine. Your way it doesn't sound polite to me.' <i>(1978,Glory and the Dream, The,5</i>)

<i>verb</i>. [Rural] [sheepdogs] to worry or nudge sheep.

### sparrowhawking

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] [sheepdogs] a frenzied rushing at sheep and a possible biting of them.

>  <b>HARTLEY</b> Sparrowhawking or running off the sheep is a serious fault. <i>(1949,Shepherd's Dogs, The,72</i>)

>  <b>LOUGHNAN</b> It [skiting] is not looked upon as a vice but more as showing playfulness. It thus differs from sparrowhawking. <i>(1981,Loughnan Glossary,73</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>.

>  <b>HARTLEY</b> <i>Sparrow-hawking</i> or running off the sheep is a serious fault. The over-anxious, highly-strung dog will show his state of excitement by rushing pell-mell at the movement of the sheep. <i>(1949,Shepherd's Dogs, The,72</i>)

### spawn

 
<i>noun</i>.

>  <b>WEEKES</b> A very strange appearance presented itself in the water this morning - streaks of a muddy yellow colour extending for miles. Supposing it to be caused by animalculae I had a bucketful drawn on deck. The water was full of them, having a transparent body with a row of yellow spots round the head. They had long tentaculae, and moved briskly through the water backwards, which motion was effected by ejecting water from two openings situated at the base of the tentaculae. These creatures are generally called [32] `spawn' by sailors; being by them considered the spawn of fish and the food of whales. <i>(Feb 3, 1841,Journal</i>) [NOTES: 1841 Feb 3 Weekes Journal in 1940 Establishment of New Plymouth 31-32]

<i>abbreviation</i>. [acronym] South Pacific Convergence Zone

### speak up

 
<i>exclamation</i>. [Rural] a command given to a dog to bark.

>  <b>GIBSON</b> I made the dogs speak up (bark) but the reply was only another weak single bark. <i>(1990,Among the High Hills of Canterbury,76</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>. [Rural] [pig or deer hunting dogs] to bark when they have found their quarry.

### spear

 
<i>verb</i>.

<i>noun</i>. applied to Maori or Moriori weapons (often erroneously)

>  Yesterday morning on opening the Lands Court, after two days' adjournment to give the natives time to send in their names for certificates for the Kaingaroa Block lately passed through the Court, and awarded to several hapus, the Tapuaka and Ngatipakio hapus, headed by Te Pokiha, and all armed with spears and other weapons, took possession of the Court House. <i>(Aug 7, 1878,Evening Post,2</i>)

>  <b>EDGAR</b> Their Weapons consists of Spears darts and battle Axes & Patoo Patoos - the Patoo Patoo's is an instrument made of bone of large Fish or Stone -it is in shape of a battledore [cf WADDY 1]& about 16 or 18 Inches long, <i>(Feb 12, 1777,Log</i>) [NOTES: 1777 Feb 12 Edgar's Log in 1908 McNab Historical Records 2/225]

>  <b>FORSTER</b> ... we heard a loud hallooing on ... an island, which on this occasion obtained the name of Indian Island; and standing on the shore we perceived one of the natives ... He stood with a club or battle-axe in his hand, ... and behind him ... two women, each of them having a long spear. ... held a long speech ... swing round his club, on which he leaned at other times. <i>(1777,Voyage Round the World,1/137</i>)

>  But both their Spears and Clubs were subject to great variety. Some of the Spears were very long and pointed only at one end, without much neatness. Their Clubs were rough pieces of Wood, ... and a very few had two stones lashed on at one end, which gave them the appearance of a double-headed maul. <i>(Nov 29, 1791,Journal of Voyage in HMS 'Chatham'</i>) [NOTES: [a Moriori spear] 1791 Nov 29 Journal of the Chathamin 1908 McNab Historical Records 2/506]

>  <b>SAVAGE</b> The spear ... is nearly thirty feet long; it is made of hard wood, and is sometimes pointed at each extremity, but not universally. <i>(1807,New Zealand (various authors/titles),66</i>)

>  <b>SHEPHERD</b> Tommy said it was next to impossible to attack a New Zealander with a sword ... as they have a method of pushing such weapons aside ... and generally kill the person with a Maree or axe or spear before he has time to make a second thrust. <i>(Mar 24, 1826,Journal</i>) [NOTES: 1826 Mar 24 Shepherd Journal in 1940 Howard Rakiura 364]

>  <b>SHERIDAN</b> ... in former days when in battle ... [they had] only their own implements of destruction - spears, nipes, and an instrument made out of beautiful blue or green marble stone, which they call a Mary, none but a chief is allowed to take them to battle, they are very scarce and very dear. <i>(1833,Letter</i>) [NOTES: 1833 Sheridan Letter from <i>Sydney Monitor</i> in 1913 McNab Old Whaling Days 48]

>  Most of these men had their stone marees (axes) slung to their wrists, and their spears placed in order ... <i>(1835,Boultbee Journal,82,1986</i>)

>  <b>YATE</b>  <i>(1835,New Zealand (various authors/titles),112</i>)

>  <b>TREGEAR</b> The principal weapon of the Maori warrior was the spear (<i>tao</i>). A short spear of from four to six feet in length was the almost invariable appurtenance of a chief ... <i>(1904,Maori Race, The,308</i>)

>  Planted Ake rautangi [dodona viscosa] the leaves that weep for ever. The wood of this tree, not a large tree, is hard and tough and took a keen edge and was cultivated by the Maori for spears and battle axes. <i>(Jul 20, 1913,Chudleigh Diary,463,1950</i>)

>  With his 'mere,' Tohi smites; / With his spear, brave Mohi fights. <i>(Nov 2, 1892,Observer (Auckland),17</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>. gum-spear

The `spear' is simply a spike of iron, about a foot long, on the end of a pole ... <i>(1873,Wonderland of the Antipodes,54</i>)

>  <b>HAY</b> For work, each man straggles about all day by himself, with his spear and spade and such. He tries every likely looking place with his spear, which is simply an iron rod, sharp at one end, and with a wooden handle at the other. <i>(1882,Brighter Britain,2/26</i>)

>  The spear is a long, slender piece of steel, four-sided and tapering to a point. When set in a handle it is easily driven into the soft ground, and the grating of the point will tell when it has touched gum. <i>(1901,NZ Illustrated Magazine,3/208</i>)

In the Matukituki Valley, `Bayonette-grass' forms an undergrowth in a dense scrub of prickly thorn .. <i>(1868,Contributions to NZ Botany,49</i>)

### special

 
<i>noun</i>. a special constable in the NZ Wars

<i>noun</i>. any of the rural recruits sworn in to control urban strikers, especially in the 1913 labour troubles (collectively also called Massey's Cossacks q.v.)

[NOTES: ?dateline -->in the 1932 riots We didn't know what a `Specials' were, but up and down Queen St were groups of men wearing white arm-bands and carrying clubs.]

>  <b>FRASER</b> Many were under 21, and joined the 'Specials' for the lark and the baton. <i>(1952,Ungrateful People,46</i>) [NOTES: Pagination from 1985 edition.]

>  <b>BOOTH</b> The Specials! The hatred was still heavy in my father's voice when he talked about them 40 years later... For my father none of that erased Freyberg's part as a Special who volunteered to battle the workers. <i>(1997,Deadline : My Story,28</i>)

>  <b>BODDY & MATTHEWS</b> Some of the unhappy 'specials', nursing batons completely unloaded, were viewing pictures in the Drill hall, and made no secret of the fact that they found it all very tame. <i>(1991,Disputed Ground,272</i>)

>  During the day the "specials" sanded the waterfront streets for the benefit of their mounts. <i>(Nov 17, 1938,NZ Observer,10</i>)

>  <b>HYDE</b> In a theatre, a suave `special' came on at the interval of an amateur first night ... to request the audience not to go out at the moment. <i>(1934,Journalese,60</i>)

>  <b>HYDE</b> 1913 brought Prime Minister Bill Massey's cockits [sic = cockies?) riding into town - strike-breakers armed with pick-handles ... On the other hand, if one of the `cocky' specials fell among strangers ... he might be wary of the boots that [52] would as soon kick in a strike-breaker's head as not. <i>(1936,Passport to Hell,51</i>)

>  <b>LAWLOR</b> I found myself mixed up with a violent mob intent on doing harm to the "specials". <i>(1935,Confessions of a Journalist,20</i>)

>  <b>HYDE</b> not intended `Back in 1913, I did time for crowning a special that cracked my mate in the great strike. <i>(1938,Nor the Years Condemn,171</i>)

>  <b>FRASER</b> Forty-five people were charged as a result of the riots, including one special constable. <i>`He was acting as a special,' </i>said the police in evidence,<i> `and had a rifle on his shoulder and a baton in his hand.' </i> <i>(1952,Ungrateful People,48</i>) [NOTES: [In 1932 15 April ?NZ Herald]]

>  There are those who remember him [Tregear] during the 1913 strike standing with blazing eyes in Cuba Street and shaking his fists at the mounted `specials' shouting: `Go home! Go home, you - scabs!' <i>(Feb 1953,Here & Now,14</i>)

>  <b>SINCLAIR</b> .. a rioter running up a back street, screaming hysterically, `The `Specials' are coming!' ... The Government passed repressive legislation annulling the traditional safeguards of personal liberty. <i>(1959,History of New Zealand,250</i>)

>  <b>McLENAGHAN</b> I got mixed up in a stoush up the street with the police, and the specials. <i>(1976,Travelling Man,152</i>)

>  <b>PUGSLEY</b> ... Massey started enrolling 2000 special constables from the country districts [to counter wharf strikes in 1913]. ... Massey's `Specials' were largely Territorial Force. ... They rode in as `Massey's Cossacks' <i>(1984,Gallipoli: the New Zealand Story,43</i>)

>  <b>OWEN & PERKINS</b> (George Davies, Wellington) [caption] Strikers scattering as mounted `specials' (`Massey's Cossacks') gallop up Featherston Street during the General Strike of 1913. <i>(1986,Speaking for Ourselves,102</i>)

>  <b>SCOTT</b> Violet Helen ... married Douglas Cromwell Snelling of Maungaturoto, farmer, Boer War veteran and leader of a group of mounted specials who rode to Auckland to break the 1913 waterfront strike. <i>(1987,Seven Lives on Salt River,84</i>)

>  An unaccompanied special, on foot, was suddenly aware of a man darting out from behind a bridge and hissing "Scab" at him. <i>(Dec 6, 1913,NZ Observer,5</i>)

[fn.] 15. ### splendid perch

>  <b>PAUL</b> <i>Splendid perch Callanthias allporti </i>Southern Australia and New Zealand. Sometimes called Allport's perch, but the name splendid is more appropriate, as it is a very colourful and variable species. <i>(1986,NZ Fishes: An Identification Guide,85</i>)

>  <b>AYLING</b> <i>SPLENDID PERCH Callanthias allporti</i> The male splendid perch is surely one of the most colourful of the fishes found in the New Zealand region. ... In New Zealand they are only found off the east coast from North Cape to East Cape ... <i>(1982,Collins Guide,208,1984</i>)

>  <b>SUTTON-SMITH</b> Some of the typical terms used in marbles referred to the act of shooting and the movement of the marbles. Those related to ways of shooting marbles were cribbing, firsts, fudging, funks, funnicks, funnigans, flunks, forces, knee-high, knuckle-down-stiff, knuckles, and lasts. Terms connected with the movement of the marbles were: cannons, clears, dead-stick, double-hits, fires, funs, gees, haystacks, in smug, keeps, kills, kisses, lay-ups, manyes, ones, pink, ringer, rolls, scat, screws, skinned, skun, spiders, sported-off, stays, stops, tracks, throughs. <i>(1972,Folkgames of Children,175</i>)

>  In the greater Christchurch City area (including the Port Hills) there are, or have been inrecent times, at least four (possibly five) species of lizard; two species of gecko,<i>Hoplodactylus maculatus</i> (common gecko) and <i>Naultinus gemmeus</i> (jewelled gecko), andtwo species of skink,<i>Oligosoma lineoocellatum</i> (spotted skink) and <i>Oligosoma spp.("common" species)</i> ... <i>(1996,Internet - see Notes</i>) [NOTES: http://researcharchive.lincoln.ac.nz/dspace/bitstream/10182/676/1/wmr_9.pdf]

>  <b>Tony Jewell</b> Recently published genetic data suggests that the spotted skink (as here defined) involves three distinct species ... However, despite being separated by very deep levels of genetic divergence, the species remain externally indistinguishable and further work is needed before they can be separated. <i>(2008,Reptiles and Amphibians of New Zealand</i>)

>  Almost half of New Zealand's reptiles are threatened or endangered. It is now illegal to handle or keep in captivity any native lizard without a permit from the Department of Conservation. Some, such as the spotted skink (<i>Oligosoma lineoocellatum</i>), are still widespread, although their numbers are probably dwindling. <i>(2009,Internet - see Notes</i>) [NOTES: http://www.wildaboutnz.co.nz/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=85:lizards&catid=27:land-animals&Itemid=78]

>  The Landcare Research team has sought answers through an intensive study of two species: the speckled skink Oligosoma infrapunctatum and the green spotted skink Oligosoma lineocellatum. <i>(Dec 1997,Internet - see Notes</i>) [NOTES: http://nzsm.webcentre.co.nz/article888.htm  New Zealand Science Monthly Online]

>  Spotted skinks also have a scattered distribution indicating that they may once havebeen widespread in lowland areas of the southern North Island south of HawkeBay. Spotted skinks are known from about 10 sites on the mainland North Islandfrom Napier, the Wairarapa and Wellington areas ... The species is also foundon islands in Wellington Harbour .. on islands in the MarlboroughSounds and is widespread in the eastern South Island ... In the North Island, spotted skinks coexist with brown, speckled and common skinks. <i>(2002,Internet - see Notes</i>) [NOTES: http://www.doc.govt.nz/upload/documents/science-and-technical/TSRP48.pdf  Department of Conservation Te Papa Atawhai]

>  <b>Spotted skink</b>: Oligosoma lineoocellatum, 111mm in length from snout to vent (minus tail).  It is much bigger than the common skink which is 73mm.  The king of the lizards in Ponatahi Lizard Sanctuary on Tim Hewitt's farm, he says he first saw them in the 1960s in their hundreds, but now they're rare. <i>(Aug 5, 2009,Wairarapa News,2</i>)

>  It will take us between five and ten years to get the populations up.  The spotted skink, for example, only breeds after aged [sic] three." <i>(Aug 5, 2009,Wairarapa News,2</i>)

>  "Without more help, saving the spotted skink and other lizards would be an uphill battle," he says.  "We needed something to keep the predators out of the area, so we decided to build a predator-proof fence." <i>(Aug 5, 2009,Wairarapa News,2</i>)

>  " .. this is the only site away from the coastal margin where spotted skink remains part of the fauna and is a reminder of the value that these small patches of remnant vegetation provide." <i>(Aug 5, 2009,Wairarapa News,2</i>)

Any alcoholic drinks, but usually spirits. The verbal forms `to spot' and `spotting' were common. <i>(1947,All Part of the Game,84</i>) [NOTES: `School Picnic [check title - not `Big Game'???]]

>  <b>CHERRILL</b> Pa wouldn't have got into the way of spotting the way he has ... . <i>(1950,Story of a NZ Sheepfarm,73</i>)

>  <b>HARTLEY</b> Mother believed dancing was worldly if not sinful, and she was frightened that we might start `spotting'. Mother's twin fears were carnal sin and having a `spot'. <i>(1987,Swagger on Our Doorstep,180</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>.

See: cf. spot v., spoiling; gridironing

>  <b>OLIVER</b> The runholder was protected against intruders: cottages, fences and homesteads gave him a pre-emptive right over a set number of contiguous acres. Fences and cottages could be so disposed as to give the runholder rights over the best of the land - sources of water and wood, strips surrounding isolated and thus inaccessible pockets. `Grid-ironing' and `spotting', as these selective practices were called, were certainly used by many runholders to tie up large areas, but probably not to the extent alleged by horrified land tenure radicals in later years. <i>(1968,Story of New Zealand, The,108</i>)

>  <b>CRAWFORD</b> `Gridironing' was the practice of buying twenty acre sections fronting on a road, so spaced as to leave sections of nineteen acres between them, and as these had to be auctioned the small farmer stood litttle chance of outbidding the run-holder who usually retained them without having to purchase them. `Spotting' was buying up key positions, fertile land, and leaving the barren, water courses, entrances to valleys, road lines, ... . <i>(1949,Sheep and Sheepmen of Canterbury,94</i>)

>  <b>SCOTTER</b> When investigating the change from pastoral lease to freehold in any locality, the student, brought up on Pember Reeves (see e.g. S.E.I. [State Experiments 1902] 234) searches immediately for evidences of the methods by which the runholder retained his grasp of the land. These practices called gridironing and spotting can be defended: there is no need to do so here. If spotting is practiced - the purchase of selected areas with water and shelter for the control this gave over the surrounding country - a study of the Crown grant index maps and of the dates of the original titles supplies no evidence of it. <i>(1948,Run, Estate and Farm,13</i>)

>  <b>CARR</b> The practice of which I speak is called in New Zealand <i>`spotting'</i> or <i>`spoiling'</i> country. [???a verbal not nominal use] <i>(1856,Waste Lands of Wellington, The,30</i>)

>  <i>Green</i>, one of the settlers, is endeavouring to purchase land in various places <i>spotting ... . </i> <i>(1865,McLean Papers,25/132 [1866 xxv/139]</i>) [NOTES: (Harris, Tauranga)]

>  <b>CRAWFORD</b> McLean brought to light some of the pitfalls of spot freeholding when he wrote in September 1970: The promiscuous `spotting' of this run with small blocks of freehold ... [sic] may have in a measure attained the primary object of excluding extensive purchase ... <i>(1981,Station Years,47</i>) [NOTES: 1870 Sep in 1981 Crawford Station Years 47]

>  <b>MORRIS</b> <i>Spotting, n.</i> New Zealand equivalent for the Australian `picking the eyes out,' and `peacocking.' Under <i>Free-selection</i> (q.v.), the squatter spotted his run, purchasing choice spots. <i>(1898,Austral English,431</i>)

>  spotting <i>n</i>. selecting the best parts of an area; peacocking.-spot v.t. <i>(1929,Whitcombe's Etym. Dict. Aust-NZ Suppl.,11</i>)

>  <b>BURDON</b> The other and yet more harmful method was to buy isolated sections all over a run to prevent or hinder large purchases by anyone else; to pick out the fertile and leave the barren; to take the grain and leave the husk. This was called `spotting.' <i>(1938,High Country,123</i>)

>  <b>BAKER</b> <i>Spotting</i> was applied to provinces other than Canterbury ... It was probably formed on the basis of the Australian terms <i>pick the eyes out of the country</i> and <i>peacocking. </i> <i>(1941,NZ Slang,26</i>)

>  <b>SINCLAIR</b> `Spotting' was the purchase of strategic points, such as the mouth of a gorge, river-banks and other watering-places, so as to exclude rivals from large areas of adjacent land. <i>(1959,History of New Zealand,156</i>)

>  <i>spotting N.</i>  in New Zealand selecting the choicest parts of an area, picking the eyes out and leaving the poorer parts. See gridironing. <i>(1966,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Whitcombe's),625</i>)

>  <i>spotting ... n.</i> in N.Z., selecting the choicest parts of an area, picking the eyes out, and leaving the poorer parts. See <i>gridironing. </i> <i>(1968,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Collins),18</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a purchase of scattered strategic and productive areas of land to dissuade other purchasers.

>  <b>FULLER</b> For the capitalist, by what is colonially termed 'spotting a Run', that is, picking out parts of it only to buy, may command the pasturage of the whole of the remaining portion ... <i>(1859,Five Years' Residence in New Zealand,72</i>)

>  <b>MORRIS</b> spotting. New Zealand equivalent for the Australian 'picking the eyes out' and 'peacocking.' <i>(1898,Austral English,431</i>)

>  <b>STEWART</b> The squatters contended that they had to adopt all these expedients of spotting and gridironing in self-protection. <i>(1940,William Rolleston: a New Zealand statesman,61</i>)

>  <b>BAKER</b> With the opening up of new land in this country .. a host of new expressions came into being, among them the Canterbury Pilgrims, shagroons, prophets, pre-Adamites, v-hut, gridironing, and spotting. <i>(1941,NZ Slang,24</i>)

>  The method of either gridironing, that is buying up the freehold of strategic parts around, or spotting, buying the strategic and fertile patches of an area that was customary with hill country settlers of the early days, was adapted by Mr Hugh Duff when taking up Whakarara ... <i>(Nov 15, 1952,Weekly News,33</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] [aerial mustering] the sighting of stragglers and stray stock.

>  A Cattle Muster on Molesworth. With the spotting we've missed seventeen. <i>(May 4, 2000,Country Calendar (TVNZ)</i>)

>  <b>DOMINY</b> Now on occasion, when spotting or straggling, some run-holders save time by using a helicopter to drop them in the back country. <i>(2001,Calling the Station Home,169</i>)

### spray dip

 
<i>noun</i>.

>  Warekauhau has a spray dip so the sheep are not actually dunked. <i>(1987,Country Calendar (TVNZ),124</i>)

### spray-dip

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a system of cleansing sheep of keds, lice and other parasites using an overhead spray.

See: sheep shower

>  <b>GASCOIGNE</b> The introduction of spray-dips a few years ago, whereby sheep arerun through on the level or held in a tank while the spray jets function, made an easy task of dipping. <i>(1965,From the Top of a Hill,33</i>)

>  <b>GASCOIGNE</b> But spray-dips, for better or worse, were still in the future in this last year of Manu's stewardship with me. <i>(1965,From the Top of a Hill,34</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>. [Rural] to spray animals with insecticide.

>  <b>COOP</b> The ideal solution to the dipping problem would be to spray-dip off shears ... <i>(1959,Shearing Ewes before Lambing,26</i>)

### spray-dipping

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] the spraying of sheep with an anti-insecticide.

[NOTES: anti?-insecticide]

>  <b>COOP</b> With spray-dipping the situation is slightly different as the length of wool makes penetration of the dip to the skin very difficult. <i>(1950,Shearing Ewes before Lambing,26</i>)

>  The term 'dip' is a hangover from when plunge dipping was the only option - it has latterly been joined first by spray-dipping and now by the pour-ons. [spray-dipping] <i>(Aug 1987,NZ Journal of Agriculture,36</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>.

>  Spray Dipping proved to be not only quicker and better, ut the cost of dipping per sheep was substantially lower than other methods. <i>(Jan 1960,NZ Dairy Exporter,20</i>)

### spraydrift

 
<i>noun</i>. airborne industrial or agricultural chemical spray

>  Spraydrift from 2,4-D butyl ester, our most widely used weedkiller, has been blamed for health problems ranging from cancer to headaches... Before his death, Foley had put forward a paper that reflected the industry's view of 2,4-D - that is, that volatile spraydrift was causing no problems and there was no need to get rid of it. <i>(Sep 7, 1996,Listener (New Zealand Listener),21</i>)

### spray-on

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a systemic stock insecticide that is sprayed on to an animal's back.

>  For prevention [of fly strike] it is often more practical for the lifestyle farmer to use long-acting pour on or spray-on treatments. <i>(2002,Lifestyle Farmer,Oct/Nov 62</i>)

### spread one's blanket

 
<i>phrase</i>. to make a (?makeshift) bed

See: spreader

>  <b>CHAMIER</b> The men ... asked permission to `spread their blankets' in the wool-shed. <i>(1891,Philosopher Dick,415</i>)

>  We are informed by a gentleman who recently visited the Thames that, notwithstanding the great number of hotels and boarding houses, the towns of Shortland and Grahamstown are at present so overfull of population that arrivals by late steamers experience the utmost difficulty in obtaining room even to spread their blankets on the bare floor. <i>(Oct 27, 1869,Daily Southern Cross,7</i>)

>  The two men spread their blankets on their vehicle's spacious interior. <i>(Jan 23, 1941,Evening Post,7</i>)

### spreader

 
<i>noun</i>.

>  <b>WAKEFIELD</b> ... `spreaders' are blankets. <i>Ibid.</i> 1/319 Thus pigs and potatoes were respectively represented by <i>"grunters"</i> and<i> "spuds"</i>; guns, powder, blankets, pipes and tobacco, by<i> "shooting sticks, dust, spreaders, steamers,"</i> and<i> "weed".</i> <i>(1845,Adventure in NZ,1/318</i>)

>  <b>PARTRIDGE</b> <i>Spreader </i>. 2. A blanket: whalers': C. 19. E.J. Wakefield' <i>Adventure in New Zealand, </i>1845 (recorded by B., 1941). <i>(1949,Dictionary of Slang Addenda,1181</i>)

>  spreader n . whalers slang for a blanket. <i>(1968,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Collins),18</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>.

>  <b>SLATTER</b> Some of his best days had been spent working as a postal assistant ... He had been a spreader in the mailroom and a dragger on the landing. <i>(1968,Pagan Game, The,85</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>.

>  <b>HENDERSON</b> SPREADER: Three-foot stout stick fitted to rear of horses' trace chains to keep chains apart. <i>(1961,Friends in Chains,189</i>) [NOTES: c1900-1920 A Teamster's Glossary in 1961 Henderson Friends In Chains 189]



 
<i>noun</i>. see cit.

>  <b>GORDON</b> <i>Spreaders </i>: the hooks and bar for spreading back legs. <i>(May 27, 1951,Personal Communication</i>) [NOTES: ca1951 May 17 Feilding Freezing Works terms p.c. Colin Gordon]



 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a metal device used in dressing a mutton carcass.

>  <b>LOUGHNAN</b> spreader: a metal device to hold the forelegs of a mutton carcass apart to facilitate some of the dressing, particularly the Y-cut. <i>(1981,Loughnan Glossary,77</i>)

### spreader board

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a board fitted at the rear of a konaki, sledge or trailer, for the even spreading of animal manure on to paddocks.

>  The types of spreader boards in use are many and varied, some being more efficient than others. ..In this case the spreader board is 18in. to 24in. wide and 6 ft.long. The manure falls into this box and thus finds it way out through the opening between the front of the box and the spreader board ... <i>(May 15, 1945,NZ Journal of Agriculture,513</i>)

### spread-man

 
<i>noun</i>. one who inserts spreaders between the back legs of carcases

>  <b>GORDON</b> <i>Spread-men</i>: those who put in <i>spreaders</i>. <i>(May 17, 1951,Personal Communication</i>) [NOTES: ca1951 May 17 Feilding Freezing Works terms p.c. Colin Gordon]

### spree

 
<i>noun</i>. in NZ from c1840 used for happy drinking bouts, as well as for shearers' and sailors' drunken orgies:

>  <b>BEST</b> [On Lieutenant Shortland's show of official force to Wellington colonists, 18--] `You may easily imagine how disappointed I was that the [Wellington] Council did not shew [sic] fight. It would have been such a spree to have blown up their magazine and besides that I should have been entitled to ?10 and 9d. per diem tentage and forage money for actual service and should also have had the pleasure of licking them, instead of which no sooner did we appear than they all sneaked off.' <i>(1843,Letter</i>) [NOTES: a1843 (1837-1843) Best's letters in Mitchell Library undated newspaper article in Journal (1966) 410]

>  <b>CAMPBELL</b> Sailors having ... a harsh captain, or a desire for a <i>spree</i>. <i>(1840,Present State of NZ,24</i>)

>  ... he is altogether an adept at Colonial life. Instance, when he commences a drunken sprey (as he calls it) he invariably puts all his money into the soles of his shoes or boots, excepting that portion he intends spending .... <i>(Jan 24, 1852,Journal</i>) [NOTES: 1852 Jan 24 Monson's Prison Journal in 1978 Locke The Gaoler 54]

>  <b>RICHARDS</b> ... and after, perhaps three years of fearful hardship, so much of the [sealers'] money as might be uncondemned would be dissipated in Sydney in a few days' `spree'. <i>(1852,Whaling and Sealing,5</i>) [NOTES: 1843 May 2 in 1863 C.Heaphy `A Chapter on Sealing' Southern Monthly Magazine June I/No 4 pp173-176 in 1982 Richards Whaling and Sealing 5]

>  <b>ANTHONY</b> Mark, do you know this, I believe I'll have to break out in a good old woolly spree, pretty soon. <i>(1936,Follow the Call,102</i>)

>  <b>PHILLIPPS</b> J.P. who has been on the spree at W.W. is laid up with a bad head in consequence <i>(Apr 28, 1867,Journal Kept at Rockwood and the Point,101</i>)

>  <b>WOOD</b> Rain came at last, and with it money, and Jim settled down to a regular spree. <i>(1875,Waiting for the Mail,106</i>)

>  English people are given to associating the idea of a `spree' with that of a bacchanal orgy. Not so We. With us the word is simply colonial for a festivity of any kind, public or private. And whatever may be the primary object of a spree, it is pretty certain to end with a dance. <i>(1882,Brighter Britain,1/272</i>)

>  <b>BEATTIE</b> A remittance man who was in receipt of at least [pounds]400 a year from Home would go on a spree and drink [pounds]5 away every day ... <i>(1939,First White Boy Born in Otago,55</i>)

>  <b>SLATTER</b> I had made the money as they told me I would. So then I spent it. Not in a sudden spree like shearers come to town, but in a deliberate determination to go under and stay under. <i>(1959,Gun in My Hand, A,13</i>)

>  <b>MANTELL</b> Lucky we found it [an abandoned car] first ... Before some larrikins commandeered it for a joy riding spree.' <i>(1980,Murder or Three, A,78</i>)

>  <b>ROCHFORT</b> [We] were shortly lulled to sleep by the heavy breathing of several sailors, who had evidently just come home from a `spree'. <i>(1853,Adventures of a Surveyor,19</i>)

>  <b>THATCHER</b> (The Caledonian Gathering) What a jolly spree the other day,/ Don't think that I am blathering,/ I'll give you just a short account/ Of the Caledonian gathering./ <i>(1864,Invercargill Minstrel,5</i>)

>  We hope his conscience pricks him, andthat he will spend all profits made on a"spree" for the boys. <i>(Mar 14, 1917,Chronicles NZEF,II/14 : 33</i>)

### spree-up

 
<i>noun</i>.

>  <b>SYDER & HODGETTS</b> A convivial gathering. .in 4;`Come round on Saturday night. We're having a bit of a spree-up because it's Tommy's last night before he goes. The beer's fixed up, bring your sax though, of course.' <i>(1962,Australian & NZ English [TS],979,1974</i>) [NOTES: (1962-63)1974 Syder and Hodgetts Aust. and NZ English [TS] 979]

### sprig

 
<i>noun</i>.

[NOTES: Jim Blakeley (508 College St, Palmerston North, 5301; blakeley@ihug.co.nz) remembers pre-WWII usage of "sprigs" as opposed to "studs" in Scotland re soccor boots, also used with regard to golf shoes. "Am almost certain that the word was also used to describe the small nails that cobblers used in repairing leather shoes. Possibly derived from sprig of heather??" Alan Burnett (aged 75) writes from 21 Hector St, Herne Bay, (2/10/1999) that when he was a child in Scotland aged about 10 "we nailed SPRIGS on our soccer boots - obtained from the local cobbler.]

>  Men studied their sprigs intently. <i>(Aug 4, 1984,Listener (New Zealand Listener),23</i>)

>  <b>CONEY</b> The English malthoid... almost trips me,dragging at my sprigs... <i>Ibid</i>. 124Like flies around an Australian, the sideclusters to borrow sprigs for a widerange of boots, and sprig tighteners formetric and AF dimensions. <i>(1986,Playing Mantis,112</i>)

>  ON SALE, at the Stores of the undersigned - Black and green teas .. an assortment of leather, hobnails, sprigs, &c. <i>(Mar 19, 1842,New Zealand Gazette & Wellington Spectator,1</i>) [NOTES: Advert]

>  It's all right... You don't feel the sprigs when you're fit. <i>(Aug 18, 1979,Listener (New Zealand Listener),13</i>)

### spring burn

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] [S.I. high country] an annual spring burning of tussock.

>  A little surface sowing with European grasses sometimes takes place after the spring burn. <i>(Jun 15, 1910,NZ Journal of Agriculture,8</i>)

>  Spring burns cause the destruction of all the accumulated dead material of the tussocks that are acting as a soil mulch ... <i>(Jun 15, 1910,BLANK ENTRY,9</i>)

>  The spring burns lessen the general vitality of the pasture ... <i>(Jun 15, 1910,BLANK ENTRY,10</i>)

### spring burning

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] an annual burning of noxious pasture growth or tussock in spring.

>  <b>COOP</b> In places where spring burning of fern, gorse, scrub or tussock is practised, shearing in August before the burn prevents any dirt and charcoal from entering the fleece. <i>(1950,Shearing Ewes before Lambing,24</i>)

### spring calving

 
<i>noun</i>. calving in July and August

>  Most farmers plan calving for July and August (euphemistically called spring calving) to take advantage of spring grass growth, which starts in September and usually peaks in late October or November. <i>(Mar 2003,NZ Geographic,62/26</i>)

### spring creek

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a stream fed by an underground spring.

>  <b>PORTER</b> As he trotted through the shallow spring creek, he stumbled on a loose boulder. <i>(1970,Under the Nor'West Arch,30</i>)

### spring eczema

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a photosensitive skin- and liver-damaging condition in cows and calves.

>  The Waipa is believed to rise in the high snowy mountains behind Tui, which are part of a range, being a spur from the great range or backbone of this island. <i>(1838,Journal of Royal Geog. Society,8/418</i>)

>  <b>PFAFF</b> He and three mates were encamped on a leading spur running down to the river. <i>(1914,Diggers' Story, The,122</i>)

>  <b>HARPER</b> The rough spurs were where the rabbits were. <i>(1967,Kettle on the Fuchsia, The,91</i>) [NOTES: Quote from Tripp 1889]

>  <b>LANCASTER</b> I was thinking t' build on the mic-a-mic spur. <i>(1904,Sons o' Men,292</i>)

>  His house is at the foot of a high spur. <i>(Mar 22, 1873,Auckland Weekly News,20</i>)

>  <b>SY MONDS</b> The Waipa is believed to rise in the high snowy mountains behind Tui, which are part of a range, being a spur from the great range or back-bone of the island. <i>(1838,Cloudy Bay,?26,1979</i>)

>  <b>MATHEW</b> The Hills [76] are lofty ... rising rapidly ... and forming an endless variety of `spurs', which are partially clothed in Timber, but chiefly with fern alone. <i>(Mar 11, 1840,Journal</i>) [NOTES: 1840 Mar 11 F.Mathew Journal in 1940 Founding of NZ 75-76]

>  <b>WAKEFIELD</b> ...steep spurs from the high mountains ... come down into the sea. <i>(1848,Handbook for New Zealand, The,235</i>)

>  After keeping the ridge for about two miles, the path turns down a spur, which is about two miles in length, ... <i>(Jan 25, 1851,Lyttelton Times,6</i>)

>  <b>SHORTLAND</b> The descent we found more steep and rugged; the northern slope of the hill having no friendly spur near us, such as that along which we had ascended, did not offer the same facility for making a road. <i>(1851,Southern Districts of NZ,173</i>)

>  <b>W.H.S. ROBERTS</b> We often went a long way down the wrong spur, and had to return, as we could never cross any swamps between the low ridges. <i>(Aug 3, 1856,Diary</i>) [NOTES: 1856 July 3 W.H.S. Roberts Diary in 1947 Beattie Early Runholding 23]

>  looked for lambs but could find no tracks. ... he has been told ... that a small mob of weaners are just to the right of the dray spur on the rough ridge. <i>(May 2, 1861,Puketoi Station Diary</i>)

>  Went on the hills burning and Greenly lit a fire on a spur that had grass and flax six feet high on it. <i>(Oct 3, 1865,Chudleigh Diary,201,1950</i>)

>  <b>BARKER</b> ... shut in gradually from our view by spurs of hills running down to the shore, sometimes in bold steep cliffs, and again in gentle declivities, with little strips of bush or scrub growing in the steep gullies between them. <i>(1867,Station Life in NZ,116,1870</i>)

>  The scene opens on a rolling plain, flanked by rocky `spurs' of the ever-present mountains; a plain of unequal surface, broken by `terraces', and watercourses, and of varying width - irregular. <i>(1873,Wild Will Enderby,3/iii/81,(1889,1974)</i>)

>  <b>KENNAWAY</b> ... the hill-spurs get steeper, and the gorges get deeper, ... <i>(1874,Crusts: a settler's fare due south,184</i>)

>  <b>TOMLINSON</b> Long tussock-covered spurs about a mile long, reached to the top on both sides. <i>(1968,Remembered Trails,40</i>)

>  In 1868 my orders were to ... see that ... no hill or spur had more sheep on it than it could well carry. <i>(1907,TrNZI,39/73</i>)

>  Spurs are good travelling to lead to thegrassland up above. <i>(1939,Canterbury Mountaineer, The,VIII/93</i>)

>  <b>FROBISHER</b> [He] proceeded to scale the steep ferny face of the spur. <i>(1893,Sketches of Gossipton,42</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] [hill country mustering] a ridge or side hill.

>  <b>MCKEE WRIGHT</b> New fences climb the warm brown spurs to guard the scrubber ewes. <i>(1898,Station Ballads,46</i>)

>  <b>GUTHRIE-SMITH</b> .. sledged posts from Tylee's spur and cut some Kohi posts for the horse paddock. <i>(1926,Tutira,122</i>)

>  <b>MARTIN</b> If the 'face' was not large, only a top beat and bottom beat would be necessary, but usually the 'spurs' had to be sidled or traversed across by several men. <i>(1990,Forgotten Worker, The,64</i>)

>  <b>DOMINY</b> .. sheer rock above me and a grassy basin defined by steep shingly spurs ... <i>(2001,Calling the Station Home,175</i>)

<i>verb</i>. to defecate

<i>noun</i>.

<i>verb</i>. [historical] to occupy a site temporarily, as newly-arrived emigrants, or while waiting for accommodation in houses or barracks

>  We therefore squatted upon the unsurveyed portion of the Palmerston Township, and have built thereon, hoping to be able to purchase the land when surveyed and put up for sale, as very many other settlers in this district have been allowed to do during the whole period since the Manawatu Block was first purchased. <i>(Mar 20, 1872,Evening Post,2</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>. to settle on an area of public land before acquiring a legal right to it; to occupy Maori (or Crown) without any legal title (cf. SQUATTER n1). squatter a) History: a runholder who originally held land by squatting. b) a rich farmer; a station-owner. (absol or constr with on)

Years later, when I had forgotten it, I suddenly met it again, and again I recoiled. So aghast was I that I spent weeks collecting every old term for `runholders' I could, and I found thirteen, viz., `flock owners,' `flock masters,' `pastoralists,' `run holders,' `run owners,' `sheep owners,' `sheep holders,' `sheep masters,' `squatters,' `station holders,' `station owners,' `stock holders,[sic] and `stock owners.' The word `sheepmen' is a modern Americanism, and using this anachronism mars a splendid memorial. ... [12] Of all the thirteen terms found in old documents, the word `runholder' was the most used, and it is the word that I think should be substituted. <i>(1947,Early Runholding in Otago,11</i>)

>  <i> Squat&#769;.ter </i>(-t&etilde.r),<i> n. [Add.] 3 </i>. The owner or occupant of a sheep run; a sheep farmer. In Australia the word had at first the sense of a settler without title; but its use was gradually extended to persons who occupied crown land for sheep raising under a lease or a license, and afterwards to those also who held their sheep runs as freehold. Finally the word became the common name for a sheep farmer, whether occupying leasehold or freehold property. It is, however, giving way to the newer term <i> pastoralist </i>. <i>(1898,Merriam-Webster Third International,2031</i>)

### St Peter's fish

 
<i>noun</i>. John Dory

>  <b>PHILLIPPS</b> CAESIOPERCA LEPIDOPTERA (Forster).</i> Red Perch </i>. Distribution* North island coasts and northern coasts of the South Island. <i>(Jun 1921,NZ Journal of Science & Technology,4/115</i>)

>  <b>WILSON</b> JOHN DORY <i>Zeus japonicus</i>: A member of the family Zeidae, of which there are at least 6 species in New Zealand waters. Also known as St Peter's fish of kuparu (Maori). <i>Ibid.</i> 204ST. PETER'S FISH <i>another name for John Dory</i> <i>(1981,Fisherman's Bible,129</i>)

>  <b>PARROTT</b> The large circular mark on each side of the body of the John Dory gave rise in earlier days to the tradition that this fish represented the species from which St. Peter obtained tribute money; the spot on either side being regarded as inherited marks left by the Apostle's finger and thumb... Unfortunately for this interesting legend the John Dory does not inhabit the lake whence St. Peter's fish was said to have been taken. <i>(1957,Sea Anglers' Fishes of NZ,55</i>)

>  <b>DOOGUE & MORELAND</b> John Dory... <i>Zeus japonicus</i>; St Peter's fish, Kuparu. <i>(1960,Sea Anglers' Guide,201</i>)

### stabknife

>  <b>SUTTON-SMITH</b> </i>Stagknife </i> (K-31), a universal game of nineteenth-century childhood, was important because it was played with the most treasured play object of all boys, the pocket knife. Although known in nearly all parts of New Zealand by the name of Stagknife, the game was also known as Bites, Jackknife, Stabknife, Knifey, Momley Peg, and Throwing the Knife. ... There were generally two players ... who each sought to deflect the point of the pocket knife from certain parts of the body by a flick of the hand in such a way that the blade would stick firmly into the ground. ... Every movement had to be done three times. [172] Typical movements were: (1) Place the open pocket knife (loose) [name of movement] [sic] on the closed knuckles of the right hand, point the knife towards the thumb, then with a quick upward flick of the hand to the left, deflect the point of the knife into the ground. <i>(1972,Folkgames of Children,171</i>)

The water dripping from their tips releases still more calcium carbon as it hits the floor directly below, forming stalagmites, sometimes mirror images of the stalactites above. This process, repeated in its infinite variations, can produce an exquisite cave decor, a tanbtalising display of beauty comparable perhaps only with the artwork of hoar frost. But the "stals," as they are commonly known, are not just aesthetic; stored within them is a wealth of geological and climatic information. ### stamp

 
<i>noun</i>.

>  <b>McARA</b> <i>Stamps</i>: The stamps pulverised the ore after it had passed through the crushers and been reduced to minus-two-and-a-half-inch size. They crushed it to a pulp, with water, until it passed through the 10-mesh (to the linear inch) screens on the mortar-box. There were five stamps (each weighing 1250 lb) to a mortar-box and they operated at 110 drops a minute from a height of 8 ins, crushing approximately 7 tons per 24-hour-day. They were driven by a camshaft, tappets attached to the long stamp stems being lifted in a particular sequence and then the whole weight of the stamp allowed to fall on the ore. Wear of iron was approximately half a pound per ton of ore crushed; the shoes and dies were cast in the Waikino foundry. <i>(1978,Gold Mining at Waihi (Glossary),333</i>)

>  <b>NOLAN</b> <i>Stamp</i>: a heavy weight, operated by machinery, used to crush ore in a stamping battery. <i>(1983,Gold Fossicker's Handbook,113</i>)

### State farm

 
<i>noun</i>. [obsolete]

>  STATE FARMS. ... The Hon. Mr. J. Mckenzie, Minister of Lands, has successfully initiated a system of paying parties of working-men to fell bush on Crown lands, giving to these men the option of choice of lands so felled and cleared. ... A State Farm proper of about 1,000 acres has been commenced at Levin ... Fifty-two men, eight women, and twenty-five children are on the ground, the men doing the preparatory work, cutting roads ... , felling bush ... getting ready for starting the permanent homestead. ... [244] It is the intention of the Government, when, after some years, the farm has been cleared of bush and brought under cultivation, to make its working purely co-operative. ... [NOTES: see Acland's, Morris's, and Beattie's discussions]

>  <b>MORRIS</b> originally the house with the necessary buildings and home-premises of a sheep-run, and still used in that sense; but now more generally signifying the run and all that goes with it, <i>Stations</i> are distinguished as <i>Sheep-stations</i> and <i>Cattle-stations</i>. <i>(1898,Austral English,436</i>)

>  <i>Station, n.</i> Sometimes <i>sheep s., cattle- s.</i>, or <i>dairy-s</i>., (PAUL, p. 68); originally the hut, yards, and buildings where a squatter stationed himself to work his run; but now usually the whole property, including the stock and leasehold country. It has been used in both these senses in Australia (whence the word came) since the 'thirties. ([1898 Morris Austral-English]) (1) The original sense is still preserved up country, where the men always speak of <i>in at the s</i>., when they are out on the run; also in the word <i>out-s</i>. (q.v.), which has no other meaning than the house, yards etc. (2) The secondary sense of a property with freehold, leasehold, buildings, and stock. (3) Any fairly large property, carrying over 2000 or 3000 sheep. (4) Adjective as in s.horse, belonging to the owner, not to one of the man, whose horses are<i> private; s. sheep</i>, not one belonging to a neighbour; <i>s.-bred,</i> not a bought sheep. (5) Since the 1890s, auctioneers in their advertisements have taken to speaking of <i>s. lines</i> of sheep, though 70 per cent. of those so designated at the autumn ewe fairs come from farms or grazing runs. ([1898 Morris Austral-English]) <i>(Dec 16, 1933,Press, The,21</i>) [NOTES: Acland Glossary]

>  <b>BEATTIE</b> The custom in the old days was to call the buildings on a run `the station,' and the land that went with it was `the run.' On a big property you could find several `stations,' and the principal one was called `the home station,' while the others were `out-stations.' This was the old Australian usage which was carried over to New Zealand at first, but gradually the signification was altered by loosely calling the whole run a station, and then the real station became a homestead and the out-stations became shepherds' huts. In this present book it will be noticed that generally the writer has preserved the olden custom of calling the main buildings the station and the land the run. The runs over in Australia being, as a rule, much larger than those in New Zealand, the `station' and `out-station' phraseology was preserved much longer than over here, where even in advertisements in the late `fifties we see the English word `homestead' ousting the colonial word `station.' <i>(1947,Early Runholding in Otago,11</i>)

>  It is usually understood that in the early days the word `station' denoted the owner's house and its immediate buildings, while `run' meant the whole property. Strange to say, I only noted the word `station' twice, and each time with a diverse meaning. On July 21, 1865, the diary says: `Sold 17 head of cattle - remaining on station 15 head.' Then on September 11, 1865, we read: `Wilkinson returned to the Home Station.' The first of these entries means the whole run - the second the homestead or main buildings. <i>(Jul 21, 1856,Puketoi Station Diary</i>) [NOTES: 1947 Beattie Early Runholding 115 quoting 1856 July 21 Puketoi Station Diary]

So aghast was I that I spent weeks collecting every old term for `runholders' I could, and I found thirteen, viz., `flock owners,' `flock masters,' `pastoralists,' `run holders,' `run owners,' `sheep owners,' `sheep holders,' `sheep masters,' `squatters,' `station holders,' `station owners,' `stock holders,[sic] and `stock owners.' >  <b>BEATTIE</b> When I first read this inscription [in the Memorial Church, Cave], the word `sheep-men' made me involuntarily flinch. Years later, when I had forgotten it, I suddenly met it again, and again I recoiled. So aghast was I that I spent weeks collecting every old term for `runholders' I could, and I found thirteen, viz., `flock owners,' `flock masters,' `pastoralists,' `run holders,' `run owners,' `sheep owners,' `sheep holders,' `sheep masters,' `squatters,' `station holders,' `station owners,' `stock holders,[sic] and `stock owners.' The word `sheepmen' is a modern Americanism, and using this anachronism mars a splendid memorial. ... >  <b>SLATTER</b> Got the pricker with me because I put his weights up - A terrible stick man, that Tank - Woppit Upper - <i>(1968,Pagan Game, The,163</i>)

>  <b>MARSHALL</b> Hugh's father said he was renowned as a local stick man. It was some time before Hugh disassociated that comment from the fishing. <i>(1982,Master of Big Jingles,9</i>)

### stick one's bib in

 
<i>phrase</i>. to interfere in another's business, to stick one's nose in (occas. keep your bib to yourself, said to an inquisitive or interfering person).

[NOTES: ca1938 Havelock -->ca1952 Wellington Keep it quiet otherwise x willstick his bib in.]

### stick out like a Chinaman on a red bike

 
<i>phrase</i>.

[NOTES: In James McNeish's <i>Joy</i> W.Griffiths Letter of 28 Feb 1983 also a friend's grandmother in Wellington used the same expression.]

### stick out like a sore toe

 
<i>phrase</i>. to be very evident

[NOTES: 1953 Feb Stan Shaw Wellington (Fide R.Mason) (cf 1953 October English Listener `sticking out like a sore thumb.')]

### stick through

 
<i>verb</i>.

>  <b>McGILL</b> <i>stick through</i> provide somebody with a telephone connection; eg `Hold on two ticks, dearie, and I'll stick you through.' <i>(1988,Dictionary of Kiwi Slang, A,107</i>)

### stick to

 
<i>verb</i>.

See: cf. stick up to

>  The cooks on a good many of the stations, have some time or another belonged to the unfortunate class and have to mix with Tom, Dick, and Harry on the road. The swaggers think these men should stick to them as soon as they get into a job, that is, keep their tucker bags full. <i>(Jan 7, 1911,NZ Truth,289/4/6</i>)

### stick to one's muttons

 
<i>phrase</i>. to keep to what one knows well; to apply oneself assiduously

[NOTES: ca 1935 eg Stick to your muttons and don't give way He stuck to his muttons pretty well and now he's worth thousands. (C Ransom cf Fr. Retournez a nos moutons, go back to our (own) business)]

>  <b>HASTINGS</b> Stick to your muttons and don't talk tripe <i>(1942,Bright Conversations,24</i>)

### stick up

 
<i>verb</i>. to book up on credit; to put on the slate; to chalk up

[NOTES: ca1949 (Havelock) Commonly used in booking up groceries]

>  <b>THATCHER</b> The loafer ... you'll find in hotels often lingers/ And orders a glass on the bounce./ `Stick it up, you know me, it's all right' <i>(1865,Colonial Songster,30</i>)

>  <b>THATCHER</b> The loafer who ne'er soils his fingers, And of gold who won't work for an ounce, You'll find in hotels often lingers, And orders a glass on the bounce. And his tumbler with brandy half filling, He'll drink and commence then to skite; And replies when he's asked for the shilling, `Stick it up, you know me, it's all right.' <i>(1875,NZ Songster,No.3/69</i>)

>  <b>McKEE WRIGHT</b> [He was] sticking up his tucker at the store. <i>(1897,Station Ballads,19</i>) [NOTES: (`Prospector')]

>  <b>ELKINGTON</b> We then `stick up' provisions in the store. <i>(1906,Adrift in NZ,244</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>.

>  <b>McGILL</b> <i>stick up</i> to delay, hold up or bring to a standstill; used in shearing; eg `We could do without this stick up, now we're certain to be late.' <i>(1988,Dictionary of Kiwi Slang, A,107</i>)

>  The Ashburton Club travelled in an express with four horses, and one of the incidents of the journey was a "stick up" in the river. <i>(May 26, 1896,Ashburton Guardian,3</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>. in phr. stuck up with porpoises: of a whale, to be slowed by playful porpoises

>  <b>GRADY</b> <i>Stuck-up with porpoises</i> - Porpoises that have slowed a swimming whale down by playing with it. This assisted the whalers. <i>(1982,Perano Whalers</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>. to bring (a vehicle, thing, a person, a job) to a standstill (often in passive form: be, get stuck up)

[NOTES: (1) The regular word for the action of bush-rangers stopping passers-by on the highway and robbing them.(2) In the case of a bank or a station, simply to rob. [1846] (3) Humorously applied to a collector or a beggar. In `Twenty - five Years of St. Andrews' (vol. ii. p. 87), A. K. H. B. tells a story of a church dignitary, who was always collecting money for church building. When a ghost appeared at Glamis Castle, addressing the ghost, the clergyman began - that `he was most anxious to raise money for a church he was erecting; that he had a bad cold and could not well get out of bed; but that his collecting-book was on the dressing-table, and he would be `extremely obliged' for a subscription.' An Australian would have said he `stuck up' the ghost for a subscription. [1890]]

>  - if you get stuck up by any creeks you'll very likely see cattle marks ... (a creek is a stream) but there is nothing that ought to stick you up at all if you keep out of the big swamp at the bottom of the valley. <i>(Jun 1860,Forest Flora,37,1960</i>)

>  The cow and steers stuck us up at the yards so we left them in the paddock. <i>(Jul 9, 1862,Chudleigh Diary,47,1950</i>)

>  An old cow stuck me up about a mile from the stockyard ... Millett and I worked our whips well on her. When she rushed one, the other stock-whipped her. <i>(Feb 21, 1863,Chudleigh Diary,78,1950</i>)

>  <b>BUTLER</b> At last we came to a waterfall. This `stuck us up', as they say here concerning any difficulty. <i>(1863,First Year in Canterbury Settlement,64</i>)

>  <b>MEREDITH</b> We started all right [on our journey], but had not got beyond the city boundary when the horses stuck us up. <i>(1875,Adventuring in Maoriland in the Seventies,80,1935</i>)

>  <b>WHITWORTH</b> ... when we told him ... we'd been stuck up by the water, he ... said ... `Ah, stuck up, were you?' <i>(1879,Spangles and Sawdust,26</i>)

>  <b>REID</b> Push on or you will be stuck up. Not by bushrangers, ... but by time and tide which wait for no man. At the first opportunity he `stuck up the mail' ... merely to secure a passage to town <i>(1884,Rambles on the Golden Coast,73</i>)

>  <b>WILSON</b> Far more often have the rivers to be forded, as is the case with the Otira ... where ... it is so wild that the coaches are sometimes `stuck up' for days, lest in trying to cross they should be washed away. <i>(Jun 3, 1894,In the Land of the Tui,88</i>)

>  <b>HARPER</b> At present, owing to the unbridged state of the rivers and frequent rain, there is great risk of loss of time by being `stuck up' by floods. <i>(1896,Pioneer Work in the Alps of NZ,32</i>)

>  <b>MACDONALD</b> These places taken together with frequently flooded rivers ..., often `sticking us up' for hours or days at a time. <i>(1910,Reminiscences,19</i>)

>  <b>BEATTIE</b> The back blocks of Southland are not inaccessible places. Until you are stuck up by the great West Coast mountains ... you can get round ... <i>(1913,Trade Hunting,[12]</i>)

>  <b>DAVIDSON</b> The only drawback to these trips was the likelihood of being stuck up now and then by flooded rivers. <i>(1930,Sketch of His Life,75</i>)

>  <i>Stick up</i>.- Bring to a standstill. (A bushranger was said to s.u. his victims.) `If you get stuck up by any creeks ... you'll very likely see cattle marks by following the creek up and down.' (Butler A First Year in Canterbury Settlement], p. 143; [1898 Morris Austral-English]). <i>(Dec 16, 1933,Press, The</i>) [NOTES: Acland Glossary]

>  <b>MASTERS</b> When they got stuck up in trying to get over the saddle, as they invariably did, they naturally made back to get him to help them over with his horses. <i>(1959,Tales of the Mails,25</i>)

>  You see there was a judgement summons up against me and I stuck up Dr. McArthur, as I thought, in the street and explained to him if my name went in the papers and ward saw it, he might stick up my promotion. <i>(Dec 13, 1902,New Zealand Free Lance,14</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>. to hold up (a job, etc.)

>  Commenced shearing. Meikana and Piripi Nehu as press men stuck me up. I gave them five minutes and sacked them. ... I put on young Wood as pressman as he was near at hand ... and put on my two station boys as fleece boys. The shed did not stop one minute. <i>(Nov 4, 1889,Chudleigh Diary,368,1950</i>)

>  <b>DAVIN</b> You might want it to coax Pompey [a ferret] out if he sticks you up. <i>(1949,Roads from Home,161</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>. to refuse to sail (a vessel)

>  <b>PUGH WIL.LIAMS</b> <i>stick her up</i>: used among seamen when they refuse to sail a vessel. <i>(1951,Letter</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>. to stop dead; to be hindered from proceeding

>  The river was very high ..., having got over that you had to walk some way and then get into a bullock dray and cross a branch that people at home [sc. England] would look at a long time ..., the bullocks sticking up in the middle each time. <i>(Nov 4, 1865,Chudleigh Diary,203,1950</i>)

>  <b>TUCKER</b> We passed only two vehicles on the road - one being an old coach `stuck up' two years ago and left. <i>(1884,Letter from Abroad,83</i>)

>  <b>CHAMIER</b> ... one cursed lot [of sheep] stuck up in the middle of the stream. <i>Ibid.</i> 429 <i>(1891,Philosopher Dick,247</i>)

>  Two drays belonging to the Messrs. Baird of Waikouaiti, were the first to be "stuck up" in this manner, and though a stout resistance was made, the drivers were compelled to yield, and the flour was sold at the price dictated by the diggers, viz., 1s. 6d. per lb. <i>(Sep 9, 1862,Otago Daily Times,5</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>. to run up; knock up

>  Having noticed in the papers that you want a few sheds stuck up, pulled down, or some other old thing, I thought as I've nothing else to fall back on just now I'd take it on. <i>(May 6, 1911,NZ Truth,306/4/6</i>)

>  .. but sticking up boards everywhere to meet the eye of the weary traveller - "No accomodation at the shepherd's hut," or in other words, "No road through Glentilt." <i>(Aug 31, 1861,Otago Witness,5</i>)

>  They have stuck up a post in the middle of the Waitetuna river, and have defied William Naylor to come any further with the road. <i>(Jun 10, 1862,Daily Southern Cross,3</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>. to bail up (pigs)

>  <b>MEREDITH</b> It sometimes takes up to half an hour to scramble through the rough gullies to where the dogs have the pig stuck up. If the bulldog were released before reaching the quarry, he would `go in' at once, and would probably be exhausted with holding the pig before we could get there, and possibly get killed. A bailed-up pig makes periodical rushes at the baiting dogs, ... <i>Ibid.</i>  97 In the morning our dogs stuck up a mob of pigs on a small, clear-topped rise. <i>(1875,Adventuring in Maoriland in the Seventies,64,1935</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>. to accost (a person for a favour)

[NOTES: ca1951 Wellington He stuck us up for a donation]

>  <b>BODELL</b> ... one day he passed my store and I stuck him up and asked for my money, ... <i>(1890,Soldier's View of Empire, A,211,1982</i>)

>  <b>THOMPSON</b> ... he ... shtuck me oop in street ... und borrowed the rhino to file. <i>(1909,Ballads about Business,11</i>)

>  <b>HARPER</b> Suppose we stick him up tomorrow [sc. about a job]. <i>(1934,Windy Island,236</i>)

>  <b>SARGESON</b> stuck: <i>stuck him up (on the street)</i>, accosted him;<i> stuck up (by the police),</i> questioned. <i>(1964,Collected Stories,303</i>)

>  <b>BURGESS</b> ... had he attempted to stick him up Mr Fox would have shot him dead. <i>(1866,Confessions,107,1983</i>)

>  <b>FARJEON</b> `We can stick up the escort in the Black Forest', he ses ... <i>(1866,Grif: a Story of Colonial Life,7</i>)

>  <b>CLAYDON</b> I was `stuck up' - to use a favourite colonial expression - by a newly arrived immigrant from England, in a New Zealand city not long ago, and asked ... <i>(1886,Popular Handbook to NZ,10</i>)

>  You see there was a judgement summons out against me and I stuck up Dr. McArthur, as I thought, in the street and explained to him if my name went in the papers and Ward saw it, he might stick up my promotion. <i>(Dec 13, 1902,NZ Free Lance,14</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>. to hold up (a person or vehicle) and rob on the highway; thence, to rob (a bank)

>  <b>WEKEY</b> The consequence [of many leaving ill-equipped] was, that some of those who carried up provisions with them were `stuck up' on the road, and the principles of communism were practically realised on the way to the Dunstan El Dorado. The first detachment of gold-seekers gradually arrived ... <i>(1862,Otago As It Is,51</i>)

>  Two of them enter[ed] the bank after the hour of closing ... `sticking them up' <i>(1855,Maungatapu Murders,11</i>)

>  <b>NESFIELD</b> Burgess ... insisted on `sticking' the old fellow up. <i>(1881,Chequered Career,79</i>)

>  <i>Stick</i> (st&ibreve.k), <i>v. t. [Add.] To stick up. (a)</i> To detain, especially on the highway, for the purpose of robbing; as, <i>to stick up</i> a traveler or a mail coach. <i>(b)</i> To rob on the highway; also, to rob, in general. <i>(c) </i>To apply to, for money, for one's signature for a petition, or the like. <i>[Colloq.] (d)</i> to accost in the street. <i>[Colloq.] (e)</i> To pose; to puzzle. <i>[Colloq.] </i> <i>(1898,Merriam-Webster Third International,2031</i>)

>  <i>stick ... stickup</i> v.t. to hold up and rob; <i>(1929,Whitcombe's Etym. Dict. Aust-NZ Suppl.,11</i>)

>  <i>v.tr.</i> of bushrangers, to hold up and rob: whence sticker-up a bushranger: by extension any such hold-up, as of a bank. <i>(1966,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Whitcombe's),625</i>)

>  <i>stick-up v.t.</i> of bushrangers, to hold up and rob; whence sticker-up, bushranger; by extension any such hold-up, as of a bank. <i>(1968,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Collins),18</i>)

>  A local business man states that on Monday night he was stuck up by a local man with two revolvers, who apparently was not clear as to what he was doing. <i>(Apr 13, 1910,Hawera & Normanby Star,5</i>)

>  The escort is not considered safe by the diggers, who decline sending gold in bulk with an insufficient guard, to be almost certainly "stuck up" on its way to Dunedin. <i>(Sep 20, 1861,Daily Southern Cross,3</i>)

>  A sensation has been caused in this district by a Maori being struck up by an armed man at Waihua Hill, Napier road, and relieved of his horse, saddle and bridle. <i>(Oct 30, 1906,Hawera & Normanby Star,5</i>)

>  On their way they called at the smithy, stuck up the blacksmith, and took from his chest some articles of clothing and provisions, besides a double-barrelled gun, powder and shot; one rummaging the cottage, while the other stood sentry at the door. <i>(Nov 18, 1857,Nelson Examiner and New Zealand Chronicle,3</i>)

>  A[b]out nine miles from the Armed Constabulary station, the coach was stuck up by twenty or thirty natives, who rescued the prisoner from the Armed Constabulary escort. <i>(Sep 12, 1877,Evening Post,2</i>)

<i>phrase</i>. euphemism for stick (it) up your arse, to have done with (something)

### stick up to

 
<i>verb</i>.

See: also stick to

[NOTES: to make up to, make love to]

>  Who tried to steam a march on him / Or stick up to his gal, / He'd tear the villain limb from limb, / And quickly sound his knell. <i>(Nov 2, 1892,Observer (Auckland),11</i>)

### sticker

 
<i>noun</i>. fillet

>  <b>JEWELL</b> <i>Fillets</i>; Sometimes called a `sticker' or `strip' Is a strip of timber or board 1[in]x 1[in]' or 2[in]'x 1[in]' placed between layers of boards in a pile and at right angles to the boards for the purpose of separating them and facilitating the circulation of air. <i>(1948,Accounting in the Timber Industry,128</i>)

>  FILLET, used as a noun only. <i>(1952,NZ Forest Glossary</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>.

>  Thinks I, this here's a kicker, But started off again; And I found a second sticker, For no Bells could I obtain. <i>(1875,NZ Songster,No.3/63</i>) [NOTES: [anon.] Trap, Trap]



 
<i>noun</i>. a notice of a traffic offence (usually gummed onto the vehicle or `stuck' under a windscreen wiper); a bluey

>  [Mr Hannah S.M.:] Every [motorist] is annoyed when he gets a sticker. <i>(Oct 31, 1951,Evening Post,12</i>)

>  Inspectors were posted on all the main motor roads, and every motorist was pulled up and asked to produce his license.   Some did, quite a few did not, and names and addresses were taken in those uncomfortable black notebooks which inspectors and others carry.   Each car was marked by a small sticker by the inspector in order that it should not be stopped again by another inspector, but there was one driver who objected strongly to stickers, small, large, and of any colour, and before his afternoon's drive was ended he had been pulled up four times, duly noted in the black book, and presented with a sticker at each stop. <i>(Nov 16, 1925,Evening Post,8</i>)

>  Those who hold that the existing car parking regulations would work quite satisfactorily if only they were enforced can have no complaint over the activities of traffic inspectors in the central business area yesterday afternoon, for "stickers" were applied to windshields in right generous fashion. <i>(May 21, 1932,Evening Post,12</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a slaughterer of stock.

>  Alister had a brother George who was a sticker at the Smithfield freezing works. A sticker is someone who cuts the sheep's [sic] throats at the meatworks... <i>(2001,Good Bastards: the larrikin's guide to success,69</i>)

>  <b>COLIN GORDON</b> <i>Stickers:</i> butchers. <i>(May 17, 1951,Personal Communication</i>)

>  <b>LOUGHNAN</b> sticker: the slaughterman who actually slays the animal. He is still called this when killing sheep though these do not receive a stab-like thrust as do the cattle or the pigs .. retain it in a suitable position for the sticker's grisly stroke. <i>(1981,Loughnan Glossary,78</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a holder or hunting dog that keeps hold of its bail.

>  <b>BEACH</b> Tom's two dogs Tip and Wog caught a lot of pigs. They were reasonable finders and terrific stickers. <i>(1993,Over 30 Years Pig Hunting,13</i>)

### stick-fence

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a fence composed of vertical sticks of manuka or supplejack tied together top and bottom [1800s.]

>  We hadn't the money to buy wire, an' we made the stick-fence do. <i>(Mar 10, 1894,Hawera Star,4</i>)

### stickies

 
<i>noun</i>. sweets

[NOTES: ca1935 (Havelock) 1953 14-15 M A2 Thames DHS 22A STICKIES [sweets] [M7] -->nf P]

### sticking

 
<i>noun</i>. i.e. to relieve bloat; or (?bleeding) to prevent death from tutu

>  <b>NORDMEYER</b> At certain times of the year [tutu] took its toll of cattle and sheep both of which required immediate treatment by `sticking' to prevent death. <i>(1981,Waitaki: the river and its lakes,42</i>)

### sticking box

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a device that holds one beast at a time for slaughtering.

>  <b>LOUGHNAN</b> sticking box: a device which holds one beast at a time, so designed that it can roll its victim on its side and retain it in a suitable position for the sticker's grisly stroke .. sticking pen: that one which feeds the sheep into the sticking box. <i>(1981,Loughnan Glossary,78</i>)

### sticking pen

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a small enclosure to hold stock for slaughter.

>  <b>SLATTER</b> The sticking-pen far below me down the tunnelled slope from the top of the ramp. From there comes the pained lowing of goaded cattle and the sharp crack of the lethal hammer wielded by the nonchalant bloke leaning over his platform above the trapped beast. <i>Ibid.</i> 67 I'd like to see them ... racing the chain, that remorseless heartless chain. And when the last is scrubbed and the chain is switched off, going down for a shower ... I'd like to see them on the chain. Even the learners' chain. In that narrow cell of concrete with the lambs swinging in quick time up the ramp from the sticking-pen ... Lambs hooked on to the chain and progressing slowly along while the row of men standing alongside slash and tear and nick with knives while others punch briskets or pull the skins from the swinging carcases. More men rip out the guts and throw the heart and liver on to the small-goods table ... and the skins and innards and hooves and ears all go by chutes to the departments below. <i>Ibid.</i> 227 The tourists ... never see the dogs running over the backs of the sheep jammed in the saleyards or the pet sheep leading them slyly up the ramp into the sticking pen at the works ... <i>(1958,Gun in My Hand, A,12</i>)

>  <b>LOUGHNAN</b> sticking pen: that one which feeds the sheep into the sticking box. <i>(1981,Loughnan Glossary,78</i>)

>  <b>KERR</b> Freezing works yarders reward an individual sheep, called the Judas sheep, to lead others to the sticking pen. <i>(2000,High Times in the High Country,82</i>)

>  <b>DILKE</b> `Sticking up', as highway robbery is called in these colonies. <i>(1868,Greater Britain,1/336</i>)

### stilts

 
<i>noun</i>. (farmers') long plough handles

### stingray

 
<i>noun</i>. any of a group of rays, having a flat, kite-shaped body with a long, narrow tail, usually ending in three poisonous spines.

>  The native feast given at the Thames to the memory of Patora, who died about two years ago, provided by two of the chief Ngatimaru tribes, consisted of 1752 large kits of kumeras, 60 kits of taro, dried sting-ray, white bait, 79 pigs, and ten bullocks. <i>(May 29, 1875,Otago Witness,14</i>)

>  Otago Institute. .. Professor Parker then exhibited a number of recent additions to the museum ... The heart of a foetal foal, the heart of a great blue shark recently mounted, and the alimentary canals of a skate and a sting-ray were also shown. <i>(Aug 13, 1886,Otago Witness,19</i>)

>  Here "Jack" gets into the water with his bare feet, and is bitten by a sting-ray. <i>(Aug 19, 1895,Taranaki Herald,2</i>)

>  A stingray weighing 180lb was picked up by Mr. G. King while fishing off Clyde-quay Wharf yesterday, and was only landed after assistance had been rendered by several persons, using jags, boathooks, etc. <i>(Feb 14, 1911,Evening Post,8</i>)

>  I have bathed from practically every  well-known beach in New Zealand, and I know the fear in which the vicious stingray is held. <i>(Dec 8, 1938,NZ Observer,8</i>)

>  <b>DRURY</b> FISH [MET WITH IN PELORUS]. Mullet - not numerous. Sting-Ray - not very numerous. <i>(1855,Sailing Directions,68</i>)

>  One afternoon, down on the rocks, I watched a bloke reel in a dirty great stingray, and stick a steel pole through its head. <i>(Jan 31, 2004,Listener (New Zealand Listener),94</i>)

>  Looking into the shallow, limpid water, might be seen the stingaree (trigon thalassa) lying on the sand bottom, like a large fryingpan. <i>(Nov 5, 1887,Auckland Weekly News,7</i>)

>  In the last 15 years two girls have been killed by stingarees. <i>(Feb 1962,Sea Spray,73</i>)
