### stinkie

 
<i>noun</i>. an inferior (often clay) marble

See: cf. stinker

>  Bartering 12 stinkies for your second-best glassie. <i>(Sep 9, 1935,Evening Post,8</i>)

>  <b>HISLOP</b> I suppose at that time [c1860s goldrush] I would be more interested in grabbing my `dumps' out of the ring at school, when some quick eye had noticed that a young pointer had tried to get away with placing a stinkie or a chalkie into play with the rest of his marbles. The `Grab your dumps' was the roar, as we all rushed in for our own, and anybody else's one could get. <i>(1943,Pure Gold,22</i>)

>  <b>SUTTON-SMITH</b> Marbles had a language of its own. There were names for the marbles, the games, and all the various aspects of the play. There were terms for marbles such as `taw' or `shooter', referring to the marbles used to fire with; `dubs', `dates', `stakes', `dukes', or `changers', referring to the marbles put down to be fired at. Then there were the terms referring to particular kinds of marbles: for example, agates, aggies, aggotties, American alleys, blood alleys, bomb-squashers, bonies, bonsers, bottlies, bull's eyes, bum-squashers, cat's eyes, chinkies, connies, duckies, eggies, glassies, Greeks, milkies, molly-bars, mulley-bars [mullibars: large marbles], peelies, peewees, piss-wees, pretties, Scotties, Scottish alleys, smokies, stinkies, stonies, stripies, tom-bobblers, white alleys, and in more recent years ball-bearings, chippies, plastics, and woodies. <i>(1972,Folkgames of Children,174</i>)

>  <b>KEITH & MAIN</b> Marbles were the currency of childhood and there were an astonishing number of names for them, some referring to the material or colour, others to value or function in the game. There were agates, aggies, American alleys, blood alleys, bomb-squashers, bonies, bonsers, bottlies, bull's eyes, bum-squashers, cats-eye, [sic] chinkies, connies, duckies, eggies, glassies, Greeks, milkies, mollies, peelies, peewees, pisswees, pretties, Scotties, smokies, stinkies, stonies, stripies, tom-bobblers and whities. The march of technology added ball bearings - ballies or steelies - which were unbeatable when it came to smashing an opponent's miserable glassie. World War II[roman] brought `clayeys' often imperfectly spherical they were pathetic terracotta substitutes for real marbles. <i>(1984,Yesterdays in Maoriland,288</i>)

>  Stinkies - these were marbles made from clay, they did not work very well. <i>(1987,Alfredton,75</i>) [NOTES: Quote from c1935]

>  <b>PARK</b> One steelie to twenty-four ordinary clay stinkers was what I charged, and a fair price it was. <i>(1992,Fence Around the Cuckoo,62</i>)

>  <b>ADSETT</b> Sixpence was a hell of a lot of money when you come to think of it. Worth about twenty marbles, more if they were only stinkies. <i>(1962,Magpie Sings, A,124</i>)

<i>noun</i>. a thin gruel made of flour, sugar, and boiling water

### stirrer

 
<i>noun</i>.

See: -

[NOTES: First heard by HWO in the early 1970s in Wellington, and possibly popularised by frequent use applied to Robert Muldoon on account of his aggressive style]

>  That an agent should be employed to transmit intelligence, who is notoriously the mouthpiece of certain cliques, and subservient to the influence of certain individuals, while he is the stirrer up of strife between local bodies, and at the same time the exponent of the views of a member of the most unreliable ministry New Zealand has ever seen, is simply unheard of. <i>(May 16, 1878,Wanganui Chronicle,2</i>)

>  Nearly all low-income earners are trade unionists and we all know what trade unionists are - commie stirrers determined to bring down the government. <i>(Nov 6, 1982,Listener (New Zealand Listener),80</i>)

>  These changes were often spearheaded by blind "stirrers" and "trouble makers". <i>(May 31, 1992,Dominion Sunday Times,24</i>)

>  Debate is of course an essential step in the development of geological ideas, and most of us owe a great deal to the many stirrers, and to the arch-stirrer himself, of that time. <i>(Oct 1980,Geological Society of NZ Newsletter,50/3</i>)

>  <i>stirrer ... NZ & Austral. colloq.</i> political agitator, troublemaker. <i>(1986,NZ Pocket Oxford Dictionary,755</i>) [NOTES: [nf. 1982 Collins Concise Eng. Dict.; 1985 Collins NZ Compact Dict. 474]]

>  <b>McGILL</b> <i>stirrer </i> troublemaker, especially in politics; eg `Parkin, gentlemen, is just your typical union stirrer, kneejerk demands every time he opens his agricultural mouth.' NZA. <i>(1988,Dictionary of Kiwi Slang, A,108</i>)

>  Mr Skinner, on the subject of new industrial legislation, described Mr Muldoon as a `stirrer' <i>(Oct 24, 1972,Radio NZ / National Radio</i>) [NOTES: Oct 24 2YA Wellington, 8.30 p.m. national news]

>  He was not afraid of authority but he was not a stirrer. His provocations were incidental to caring for the losers who came to him, for shelter or for guidance. <i>(Oct 25, 1972,Dominion,4</i>)

>  So Bob Jones wrote a blank book ... and got a well known stirrer to help launch it - ... <i>(Mar 20, 1974,Dominion,Cartoon in 1982 Jones Letters 26</i>)

>  <b>SINCLAIR</b> The men behind the abortive coup were the remnants of the credit reformers, or Leeites, in the caucus of the 1930s: Mason (who detested Nash), Bill Anderton, and Nordmeyer who, while probably never a creditite, had been numbered in the ranks of the dissidents as an ambitious young `stirrer'. <i>(1976,Nash,292</i>)

>  No stirrers need apply...The SIS are looking for recruits. <i>(Nov 24, 1979,Listener (New Zealand Listener),113</i>)

>  <b>LELAND</b> <i>stirrer:</i> short for shitstirrer, a TROBLEMAKER of you don't agree with them, a crusader if you do. <i>(1980,Personal Kiwi-Yankee Dictionary, A,97</i>)

>  <b>KENNEDY</b> Was the barman right when he said that outside `stirrers' were to blame? <i>(1981,Straight from the Shoulder,24</i>)

>  <b>HULME</b> Going flat on his face in the slime, I couldn't give a damn for him, the two-faced stirrer, going to the police behind everyone's back ... [sic] <i>(1983,Bone People, The,395</i>)

>  <b>SINCLAIR</b> By 1939 the leading academic agnostic, stirrer, and radical, and soon `establishment figure', `Tommy' Hunter of Victoria, was knighted. <i>(1983,History of the University of Auckland, A,151</i>)

>  <b>MITCALFE</b> `And, if it's jus' the paper "stirring", what then?' ... `Now you jus' a "stirrer" too,' said Vaine. <i>(1985,Hey Hey Hey,108</i>)

### stock unit

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a measure of land's carrying-capacity [ the annual feed requirements of an animal, e.g. 1 ewe = 1.0 SU, 1 Jersey cow = 6.0 SU. One stock unit requires approx 520 kg of good quality pasture dry matter per year.]

>  Eighty years ago New Zealand was without grazing animals or herbage, but to-day its stock unit was 71 as compared with 100 of the Mother Country. <i>(Apr 20, 1928,Evening Post,8</i>)

>  <b>MAF</b> Stock unit .. also referred to as ewe equivalent. It is the feed requirement used as the basis of comparison for different classes and species of stock. It expresses the annual feed requirements equivalent to one 55 kg ewe rearing a single lamb. <i>(1982,MAF Agricultural Glossary,7</i>)

>  Stock units are based on the conversion ratios first recommended by Professor Coop from Linclon College in 1965. These ratios are ewes per head 1.0, hoggest [sic] 0.6, others per head 0.8, cows per head 6.0.. <i>(Aug 1984,NZ Journal of Agriculture,28</i>)

>  Steers are equivalent to about six stock units ... <i>(Sep 1986,NZ Journal of Agriculture,8</i>)

>  <b>GORDON</b> One young couple is running over 20,000 stock units in a low labour system that was established by a lot of hard work ... <i>(1987,People, Places & Paddocks,46</i>)

>  The property has been well managed by the current owners for several generations ans carries approx 7000 SU.. Assessed at 3800 SU wintered being 80% sheep and 20% cattle. <i>(Nov 10, 2001,Hawke's Bay Today,22</i>)

>  They run 8000 SU of sheep, beef and deer with the majority, 6000 SU, in sheep. [sU] <i>(2002,Wool Grower,Spring 25</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>.

>  We allude more particularly to the district of Wairarapa, the speedy acquisition of which is not only in justice due to the settlers established there, but is necessary in order that some general rules may be framed to regulate and protect the interests of stockowners, and to encourage the formation of new stations. <i>(Jan 19, 1848,New Zealand Spectator & Cook's Strait Guardian,2</i>)

>  <b>SEWELL</b> The stockowners talk big about what they mean to do one of these days in return for those pre-emptive rights which they have secured to themselves. <i>(1856,Sewell Journal 1853-1857,12</i>) [NOTES: in McIntyre (1980) Sewell Journal 1853-1857 209]

### stockperson

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a farm worker employed specifically to manage a property's stock.

[NOTES: cf stock keeper]

>  Large intensive grazing unit requires a top self motivated stockperson who has the confidence to manage approximately 1100 dairy grazers and numerous other dry stock. <i>(Mar 17, 2001,Dominion,65</i>)

>  Stockperson: a position is available for a motivated person within a progressive agribusiness specifically on a 945 ha finishing and breeding property. <i>(Nov 3, 2001,Dominion,36</i>)

>  Shepherd General : Must be motivated, a good stockperson, reliable and have a good team of dogs. <i>(Feb 9, 2002,Dominion,31</i>)

>  Stockperson wanted dead or alive 1620 hectare property, 19 kms north of Taihape ... <i>(Oct 19, 2002,Dominion Post,C19</i>)

### stock-sense

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] an ability to manage animals well and to readily assess their needs and characteristics.

>  <b>RICHARDS</b> Valerie was also a very capable rider, kind with animals and with a good 'stock-sense.' <i>(1989,Pioneer's Life, A,76</i>)

### stockwhip

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a whip used in moving stock [esp.on cattle stations where stock are unused to being driven or managed.]

>  [.. The assault for which she has now been punished consisted in her throwing some stuff from a small can over Miss Ross as the latter was leaving the stage-door of the Theatre Royal, Melbourne, and following this up by striking her a violent blow across the forehead with the heavy handle of a stockwhip.] <i>(May 8, 1901,Evening Post,5</i>)

>  <b>SCOTT</b> In those days I learned to use the stockwhip, an instrument of torture consisting of a handle about a foot long and weighted with lead and a thong, ten, twelve, or even sixteen feet long from loop to point, as the skill or ambition of its owner prompted. <i>(1922,Reminiscences of a New Chum in Otago,36</i>)

>  .. the length and weight of the blood-stained, butt-end and lead-loaded 'fall' of an old stockwhip ... <i>(Dec 31, 1964,NZ Farmer,14</i>)

>  <b>LOUGHNAN</b> Fall: the lash of a stockwhip is of plaited leather. <i>(1981,Loughnan Glossary,29</i>)

>  <b>HINDMARSH</b> Stockwhips, rattles and even oilskins had to be used to supplement the puny dog power. <i>(1997,Come Be a Pioneer,105</i>)

>  Witness, continuing, said he saw defendant cruelly whipping the horse with a short handled stockwhip, and later saw it with two gashes on its loins. <i>(Jan 19, 1894,Wanganui Herald,3</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>.

>  Richard Morrow, Parapara, was charged on the information of John Hill, with assaulting him on the previous Sunday, by striking him on the back with a stockwhip. <i>(Feb 26, 1886,Taranaki Herald,2</i>)

>  Arthur Edward Burch, aged 52, a drover, was found by his wife early this morning hanging by a stockwhip from a tree near his residence. <i>(Aug 17, 1929,Evening Post,11</i>)

>  WILL Finder of Stockwhip Handle left in 7.17 Wellington-Waterloo train Sunday please communicate with 196 Post Agency, Lower Hutt? <i>(Nov 30, 1942,Evening Post,1</i>)

>  If men or women get up on a stage and actually do something - sing, dance or crack stockwhips - well and good. <i>(Feb 27, 2000,Sunday Star Times,C6</i>)

>  At Oeo a party of drovers were refreshing themselves, their dogs and their stockwhips. <i>(Jan 1, 1887,Auckland Weekly News,7</i>)

>  A better-hearted old towser never cracked a stock-whip. <i>(1900,Auckland Weekly News,Xmas No. : 17</i>)

>  <b>HENDERSON</b> The boss had cut a blade of flax, and, having stripped it into whiitau, was making a cracker for his stockwhip. <i>(1974,Open Country Muster,178</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>.

>  <b>IHIMAERA & LONG</b> When he was better he stock-whipped Maori, nearly killed him. <i>(1982,Into the World of Light,162</i>)

>  Loafers on the State are the most despicable people in the community, and they should be stockwhipped into some sort of activity. <i>(Sep 29, 1906,NZ Truth,3</i>)

>  Can Sarah and her friends who blasphemed the name of the great Founder of Christianity day by day by putting his name to things that he never sanctioned, say that He who stockwhipped single-handed a rabble push who were defiling the Temple in Jerusalem 2000 years ago, would, had He been here in the flesh, now have shown the white feather and shirked his duty to humanity? <i>(Feb 16, 1918,NZ Truth,2</i>)

>  I have not the slightest doubt in my own mind that had the Hawera Ejectment Committee had the matter in their own hands up to now that Master Te Whiti would have been thoroughly non-plussed, for he would have found it difficult, notwithstanding their fanaticism, to get Maoris to come ploughing if one party got stock-whipped across the river, and their ploughs broken, and their bullocks impounded, as was intended, had not the Government stepped in and put the Constabulary to do the civil work of arresting them. <i>(Jul 12, 1879,Wanganui Chronicle,2</i>)

>  However, something seemed to carry him beyond the bounds of discretion, and he went on to talk the usual tommy rot about the pioneers of the old days, the present day  grey beards and white heads, concluding his reference by the startling statement that the rising generation "should be stock-whipped into the bush." <i>(Nov 30, 1896,West Coast Times,4</i>)

### stockyard

 
<i>verb</i>.

[NOTES: fig]

>  The Ohinemuri natives say that, with Tauranga on the one side, the Ngatihauas above them at Matamata, and Hauraki below them, they are "stockyarded." <i>(Nov 13, 1867,Daily Southern Cross,3</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] an enclosure for containing cattle and less often, sheep.

>  At his Stock-yards, at Evans' Bay, on Monday, October 26, 1840, at one o'clock precisely, about 60 head of Cattle, more or less, consisting of Bullocks and Cows, some with Calves by their sides. <i>(Oct 24, 1840,New Zealand Gazette & Wellington Spectator,1</i>)

>  There are good stockyards &c., complete for a dairy station. <i>(Nov 19, 1856,Lyttelton Times,11</i>)

>  Approaching the stockyard, the "pom" asked, "What is that?" <i>(Nov 16, 1929,Evening Post,21</i>)

>  LOST - Left outside Thorndon Railway Stockyards a Stockwhip. <i>(Oct 3, 1919,Evening Post,1</i>)

>  In the Mount Cook region, they had been so destructive a few years ago that the country at the head of the Hooker Valley was as dead as a much-trampled stockyard. <i>(Sep 11, 1945,Evening Post,6</i>)

>  The yard for cattle, or "stockyard" is one of the strongest and best built in the district. <i>(Jan 23, 1890,Otago Witness,7</i>)

>  <b>Owen Marshall</b> His earliest recollection was of sitting on a large post in the stockyards of a Canterbury farm, aware of dry hills twitching in the distance and cattle immediately before him. <i>(2007,Drybread,65</i>)

>  I have heard of an idiot who was driven to the poll with a stock-whip like a bullock, to a stockyard. <i>(Oct 8, 1887,Auckland Weekly News,15</i>)

>  PAVING. STOCKYARDS, COWBAILS, &C. THE undersigned is prepared to execute all kinds of the above class of work on the shortest notice. <i>(Aug 30, 1906,Hawera & Normanby Star,1</i>)

>  389 Acres open grass land, comprising some of the best land in the district; sub-divided into 5 paddocks, all watered; secure, live fences; 7-roomed dwelling, stables, stockyard, shed, etc. <i>(Feb 6, 1892,Wanganui Herald,4</i>)

>  <b>ADAMS</b> A dairy and stockyard is also attached to this station ... <i>(1853,Spring in the Canterbury Settlement, A,70</i>)

>  Now our stockyard is different from most - the only substantial part of it being the gate. <i>(1926,NZ Dairyman,137</i>)

>  <b>SHARPE</b> It [manuka] had provided the rails for a set of stockyards at one end of the holding paddock. <i>(1966,Fiordland Muster,54</i>)

>  <b>NEWTON</b> They had a good set-up with the stockyards at Riversdale <i>(1966,Boss's Story, The,27</i>)

>  She drove them.. up from the lower paddocks towards the stockyard and the cowshed. <i>(Oct 14, 1924,Otago Witness,54</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>. [Rural] to place livestock in pens or yards.

[NOTES: incl 1x citation stockyarding, verbal noun]

>  Some make a practice of stock-yarding their cattle every night, for the sake of accumulating manure for their arable land ... <i>(Jan 22, 1861,Wellington Independent,5</i>)

>  <b>KENNAWAY</b> One morning we rode down to a neighbouring station about twelve miles off, stockyarded our horses, and knocked at the station-owner's door. <i>(1874,Crusts: a settler's fare due south,110</i>)

<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a heavy, high laced leather boot.

### stopping dog

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a holding sheepdog that will stop sheep in their tracks and hold them.

>  There is no such thing now as a stopping dog on the Merino country in the South Island. If the run so described by 'Old Shepherd' was not that of a stopping dog, I would like to hear how your correspondent would improve on it. The silent heading dog is a necessity on rough country. In the old days we called them stopping dogs. Stopping dogs are still an essential on that [high] country. <i>(Mar 1931,NZ Farmer,231</i>)

>  <b>NEWTON</b> The huntaways also do the forcing and yard work. A breed now almost extinct, that is peculiar to the high country, is the 'stopping dog' which may be described as a specialist heading dog. <i>(1947,Wayleggo,13</i>)

>  Between the straight-out stopping dog and the huntaway is the handy dog. In the North Island, where the general sheep stock is predominantly the sluggish and slow-moving Romney, and the configuration easier, the straight stopping dog is useless. <i>(Nov 5, 1953,NZ Farmer,45</i>)

>  <b>NEWTON</b> Take the 'stopping dog' for instance - at one time he was almost essential in a high-country man's pack. <i>(1964,Straggle Muster,83</i>)

>  We don't know whether Mac here is a 'ringing' dog, a Shandy Gaff, a 'stoppy' dog, a 'Sunday dog' or maybe he's none of these. <i>(Dec 15, 1983,NZ Journal of Agriculture,45</i>)

>  Stoppy dog - also called a 'holding dog' .. many high country men had one in their team to corner runaways or hermits. Legend has it that if you forgot to call a good stopping dog off, it would stay on the job till one or other of the parties dropped dead. [stoppy dog] <i>(Dec 15, 1983,NZ Journal of Agriculture,46</i>)

### storm petrel

 
<i>noun</i>. (aka Jesus Christ bird, skipjack, dancing dolly, (all from its apparent ability to `walk' on water), =takahikaremoana ) a very small black seabird with a white rump, which follows ships and whose appearance was thought to announce a coming storm.

### straggle

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a small group of sheep evading muster.

>  These musterers who climbed several hundred metres around dawn to drive straggles of sheep down to the valley floor might work their way in time to be head musterer, foreman or manager, amd ultimately perhaps attain their own lease. <i>(Aug 2002,Forest & Bird,27</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>. [Rural] to find straggler sheep [and often to blade-shear bellies and under-necks so that they can walk out in a muster.]

>  <b>STRONACH</b> So after three days of mustering about the paddocks, with a dagging thrown in, we were glad to get away up Yoe Creek again to straggle the ewe country. To straggle a block of country means of course to muster in the stragglers. <i>(1953,Musterer on Molesworth,31</i>)

>  <b>WESTMACOTT</b> In bush country they have to straggle the new burns after a first muster. <i>(1977,After-Breakfast Cigar, The,145</i>)

>  <b>PETER</b> We straggle a block and trace the roughies as they usually have a double fleece. i.e. we muster for the stragglers and blade-shear bellies and under neck so they can walk out. <i>(2000,Peter Glossary</i>)

>  <b>DOMINY</b> Now on occasion, when spotting or straggling, some run-holders save time by using a helicopter to drop them in the back country. <i>(2001,Calling the Station Home,169</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>. [Rural] [stragglers and wild sheep] to wander without direction.

>  <b>GUTHRIE-SMITH</b> In one way or another hundreds of sheep thus straggled from the run. <i>(1921,Tutira,140</i>)

>  <b>WESTMACOTT</b> The sheep straggled up the valley and we followed ... <i>(1977,After-Breakfast Cigar, The,115</i>)

<i>noun</i>. [Rural] searching for straggler sheep

### straggle muster

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] sheep that have missed an initial muster, and are gathered in the straggle muster.

>  <b>RICHARDS</b> Before leaving Otupae, Roger Pearce and I had been asked if we would return in three weeks to shear the 'straggle muster.' <i>(1989,Pioneer's Life, A,47</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a secondary muster to collect stock missed in initial muster.

<i>verb</i>. [Rural] to have a second muster to gather stragglers that have missed a first or main muster.

>  <b>NEWTON</b> .. we finished up by straggle mustering the whole of the summer country again. <i>(1964,Straggle Muster,107</i>)

>  <b>MACGREGOR</b> On one occasion we were out straggle mustering for sheep missed in the main muster. <i>(1980,Dog's Life, A,12</i>)

>  <b>NEWTON</b> There was a good gang up the Ant.. at which the gang could camp during the fortnight the sheep were held there, and from which they could straggle-muster the rest of the country. <i>(1966,Boss's Story, The,38</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>. [Rural] to clear the bar at closing time.

### straggle tally

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a total number of sheep missed in an initial muster, but mustered in later.

>  <b>NEWTON</b> The other day the talk got round to 'straggle' tallies ( sheep missed in a muster.) I reckon that place must hold a world record for a straggle tally. <i>(1964,Straggle Muster,106</i>)

### straggle-mustering

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a second gathering to collect stock missed in an initial muster.

>  Straggle mustering. <i>(Feb 11, 1868,Castle Station Diary,260</i>) [NOTES: in Vance (1965) High Endeavour]

>  <b>NEWTON</b> This straggle-mustering after the autumn muster had never been practised at Mount White. <i>(1966,Boss's Story, The,38</i>)

### straggler

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] 1.a sheep or cattle beast missed by a mustering team or a sheep or cattle beast that has strayed on to a neighbouring property, more common when natural boundaries preceded fences.  2. a ewe that is late to lamb; a late-lamber. 3. a slow-moving sheep at the back of a mob.

See: hermit; double-decker; double-fleecer; stray

>  The bulk of the wools offered was made up largely of stragglers and other late shorn sheep, and its character therefore was not up to the usual average, and it could not therefore be expected to establish a high range of values ... <i>(Apr 5, 1894,Otago Witness,13</i>)

>  The lamb was found by defendant in a paddock adjoining one of his camping paddocks, and taking it to be a straggler he had it killed under a custom which he said was long prevailed of accommodation paddock owners killing stragglers and accounting for them if called upon to do so. <i>(Jun 3, 1904,Wanganui Herald,6</i>)

>  <b>ORMOND</b> A good shearing day - got through 1431 sheep - all greasy ewes with exception of stragglers from the wether block. Jan 19. David out all day clearing off stragglers. <i>(Jan 18, 1865,JD Ormond Stockbook 1864-1866</i>)

>  <b>MURISON</b> Sent Wilkinson to Drysdales to head weaners whilst Read searches for stragglers. <i>(Sep 13, 1865,Puketoi Station Diary</i>)

>  <b>MURISON</b> Shearing stragglers. <i>(Mar 29, 1867,Puketoi Station Diary</i>)

>  CHS, TS, Kite and Jim went mustering the reserve for stragglers. <i>(Mar 1, 1879,Tutira Station Diary</i>)

### Strathmore weed

 
<i>noun</i>. a shrubby native weed of spp Pimelea, poisonous to stock.

>  <b>CROWE</b> <i>Pimelea prostrata</i> Pinatoro; Strathmore weed... Part eaten : The berries. No other part of the plants should be eaten as Strathmore weed has been known to poison livestock. <i>(1997,Field Guide to Native Edible Plants of NZ,43</i>)

>  <b>LEVY</b> Strathmore weed, a low-growing shrubby plant found on poor, friable soils, if eaten when stock are forced on it in a holding paddock, may cause staggers and death, particularly if the stock are afterwards driven. <i>(1970,Grasslands of NZ,305</i>)

>  A waggon broke down at Miki Miki, Wairarapa;  the horses were turned out, and partook of "Strathmore weed," which the local horses will not touch. <i>(Sep 6, 1910,Poverty Bay Herald,3</i>)

>  I am forwarding you specimens of the Strathmore weed. I interviewed Mr Hewer, coach-proprietor, Strathmore and Stratford, re the matter. He informs me that the weed is very injurious to strange horses..This Strathmore weed proved to be two species of native plants, Pimelea lyalli and P prostrata. <i>(1900,Leaflets for Farmers,55  2</i>)

>  The first case of Strathmore weed poisoning known in the Wairarapa occurred some days ago ... <i>(Sep 21, 1908,Dominion Post,5</i>)

>  Strathmore weed <i>(Pimelea prostrata)</i> this plant is fairly widespread throughout New Zealand. <i>(Feb 24, 1966,NZ Farmer,29</i>)

>  I am forwarding you specimens of the Strathmore weed. I interviewed Mr. Hewer, coach-proprietor, Strathmore and Stratford, re the matter. He informs me that the weed is very injurious to strange horses... This Strathmore weed proved to be two species of native plants, <i>Pimelea lyalli</i> and <i>P. prostrata</i>. <i>(1900,Leaflets for Farmers,No. 55/2</i>)

>  Mr. Gooch, Stratford cab proprietor, has had the misfortune to lose a horse, the animal having been poisoned by the "Strathmore weed," about which there was some talk a little while ago. <i>(Jul 14, 1899,Hawera & Normanby Star,2</i>)

>  The first case of Strathmore weed poisoning known in the Wairarapa occurred some days ago, when out of a number of draught horses stricken two died... He noticed.. little clumps of a weed very like the garden daphne growing in the paddock where the horses had been feeding... The weed in question is native, and known by the names Mataikairanga and Strathmore. The name Strathmore was given after the name of the locality near Hawera, where the first reported case of animal sickness through eating the weed was made known some eight years ago... The first symptoms of Strathmore poisoning are loss of appetite, and then dullness. followed by tremors, staggering, distressed breathing, and convulsions, which in the severe cases are followed by death. <i>(Sep 21, 1908,Dominion,5</i>)

>  Strathmore Weed (<i>Pimelea prostrata</i>. The first outbreak.. was due to the plant <i>Pimelea prostrata</i> commonly known in the North island as "Strathmore weed". <i>(1926,NZ Journal of Agriculture,XXXIII/102</i>)

>  There are several species of <i>Pimelea</i> in New Zealand... It is known in New Zealand generally as Strathmore weed, from the name of a Taranaki town where posoning of horses was first recorded. <i>(1934,NZ Journal of Agriculture,XLIX/152</i>)

Block grazing differs from strip grazing to the extent that the herd/flock is offered pasture on a daily basis with both a front and back temporaray electric fence, and daily blocks are rectangular in shape. <i>(1999,NZ Pasture and Crop Science,156</i>)

### Subtropical Gyre

 
<i>noun</i>. an ocean current

>  New Zealand straddles the southern arm of the so-called Subtropical Gyre, the massive counter-clockwise flow of water around the South Pacific. From South America, water moves westward to Australia, turns south and strengthens as the East Australian Current; then off New South Wales it turns east as the Tasman Front, passing around Northland to spawn the weak West Auckland current (extending to Auckland) and the strong East Auckland Current (extending to East Cape). <i>(Nov 2002,Forest & Bird,306/15</i>)

### summer

 
<i>verb</i>.

See: also winter verb

>  <b>NEWTON</b> Apart from summering the ewes from weaning time until the rams go out the actual Rainbow country is now carrying only the 400-odd breeding cows. <i>(1973,Big Country,29,(1977)</i>)

>  <b>WHEELER</b> `Our 45,000 halfbreds summer high on the Nevis block,' says Frank, `and winter far below on sunny spurs.' <i>(1982,Historic Sheep Stations of NZ,7</i>)



 
<i>verb</i>. [Rural] [high country] to carry stock through the summer season on land that is unproductive, dangerous and snow-covered during winter.

>  The two-tooths are summered on the high country. <i>(Sep 27, 1951,NZ Farmer,9</i>)

>  <b>NEWTON</b> It is bushbound country, and although it is a real death trap in the winter could summer a tremendous number of sheep. <i>(1952,High Country Journey,140</i>)

>  <b>NEWTON</b> In the good old days, a fence ran from Lake Tennyson through to the Wairau and the country beyond the fence, the Rainbow block, summered the two-tooth ewes and the entire wether flock - anything up to 20,000 sheep. <i>(1952,High Country Journey,188</i>)

>  <b>NEWTON</b> St James, in those days, summered the entire wether flock on the Clarence country.. <i>(1964,Straggle Muster,6</i>)

>  <b>NEWTON</b> Mt White summer their whole flock up the Esk.. ibid. 10 The bulk of the flock is summered at the head of the Esk. <i>(1964,Straggle Muster,9</i>)

>  <b>NEWTON</b> ... it is real shingle country but, for all its harsh appearance, it summered the bulk of the wether flock ... <i>(1973,Big Country of the South Island,193</i>)

>  <b>ASPINALL</b> Mr Harry Barker summered cattle in both Aspiring and Shovel Flats. <i>(1993,Farming Under Aspiring,40</i>)

### summer country

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] [high country] land that can be grazed only in the summer when free of snow.

>  <b>MORRIS</b> Summer country n., in New Zealand (South Island) country which can be used in summer only; mountain land in Otago and Canterbury, above a certain level. <i>(1898,Austral English,444</i>)

>  Of all those stations possessing country above 3,000 ft, the grazing-ground is more or less sharply divided off into what is called 'summer country' and 'winter country.' <i>(Jun 15, 1910,NZ Journal of Agriculture,7</i>)

>  .. the merino is mustered from the summer country at levels between 7,000 ft. and 8,000 ft., and within the shadow of the glaciers. <i>(Feb 20, 1937,NZ Journal of Agriculture,98</i>)

>  <b>COOP</b> During the mid-summer and autumn the sheep are pushed up on to the 'summer country' - the highest part of the run. <i>(1949,Animal Nutrition,94</i>)

>  This is all high altitude log country - grand summer country, but subject to snow in winter. <i>(1969,Big Country of the North Island,245</i>)

>  Beyond Queenstown there is absolutely nothing but pastoral country, most of it summer country at that, which I affirm from personal knowledge cannot be profitably worked except in very extensive tracts. <i>(May 14, 1881,Otago Witness,13</i>)

>  To what Mr Duncan had said it might be answered that a flock-owner there would, for his own protection, and for stock farming an pasturing purposes, buy winter country as well as summer country. <i>(May 30, 1868,Otago Witness,7</i>)

>  This is all good summer country, and also includes some first-class land on the flat known as the Upper Taieri Flat, and adjoining what was, until last year, Patearoa Station, but which is now all cut up. <i>(Feb 8, 1905,Otago Witness,35</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] land that does not dry out in summer.

>  Good summer country with excellent stock handling facilities. <i>(May 5, 2001,Hawke's Bay Today,21</i>)



 
<i>noun</i>. a high-country farming term for an area that is usable in summer as pasture, but not in winter.

See: winter country

>  "In those cases where there is no natural boundary between winter and summer country it would on many runs be practicable to fence off the unsafe country, with a view to ensuring that sheep mustered down on to the winter country in the autumn could not drift back between storms on to unsafe country and be lost, were it not for the heavy expense involved in fencing ..." <i>(Aug 13, 1938,Evening Post,13</i>)

>  <b>MORRIS</b> <i>Summer Country, n.</i> In New Zealand (South Island), country which can be used in summer only; mountain land in Otago and Canterbury, above a certain level. <i>(1898,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Collins),444</i>)

>  <b>PERRY</b> The higher country, and that having a southerly aspect, which is likely to hold snow to some depth in the winter months, is termed `summer country', for it is unsafe for sheep in the winter, and is used only for summer grazing. <i>(1922,NZ Sheepfarming,88</i>)

>  <b>NEWTON</b> In high country a lot of the country, i.e., the hinterland and higher areas, carries too much snow to carry any sheep in the winter. Accordingly, it is only stocked in the summer and is known as `summer country.' Conversely, safe country which is saved for the winter is `winter country.' <i>(1949,High Country Days,197</i>) [NOTES: (1950),  (Gloss.)]

>  <b>STRONACH</b> This block is good summer country and splendid mustering. <i>(1953,Musterer on Molesworth,9</i>)

>  <b>SHARPE</b> ... sheep which act like that stay out on the summer country until they are either found in a `straggler muster' or buried by snow. <i>(1962,Country Occasions,123</i>)

>  <i>summer country n.</i> in South Island of New Zealand country which can be used for grazing only in summer. <i>(1966,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Whitcombe's),626</i>)

>  <b>NEWTON</b> <i>Summer country</i>: high-country run comprises summer and winter country. The former is the higher or shady country which carries a lot of snow during the winter and is then uunsafe for stock. Winter country is the lower and sunnier country on which sheep can safely be carried during the winter. <i>(1966,Boss's Story, The,189</i>) [NOTES: (Gloss.)]

>  <i>Summer country n.</i> in S. Is. of N.Z., country which can be used for grazing in summer only. <i>(1968,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Collins),19</i>)

>  <b>MCCASKILL</b> The Molesworth cows have to travel up to 120 miles moving from summer to winter country and back. <i>(1969,Molesworth,182</i>)

>  <b>WHEELER</b> In the South Island the terms `summer' and `winter' country have a very real meaning for the station owner. <i>(1973,Historic Sheep Stations NI,92</i>)

>  <b>NEWTON</b> A large proportion of the country - the shady and hindermost areas - is suitable for summer grazing only ... Such country is known as `summer country' <i>(1947,Wayleggo,14</i>)

>  <i>summ'er country n.</i> land that can only be used in the summer. <i>(1929,Whitcombe's Etym. Dict. Aust-NZ Suppl.,11</i>) [NOTES: actual dates: c1929-1936]

>  <b>GRAY</b> I rode up the Orari run ... to put a mob of sheep back on to the Blue Mountain, which is the farthest of their summer country. <i>(Feb 27, 1876,Quiet with the Hills,42</i>) [NOTES: 1876 Feb 27 Peache Jnl in 1970 Gray Quiet with the Hills 42]

### summer sickness

 
<i>noun</i>. a form of food poisoning, a usually brief but prostrating illness characterised by vomiting and diarrhoea and associated with hot weather.

[NOTES: Jim writes : Not in DNZE or overseas dictionaries available to me. the British equivalent may be <i>summer flu</i>, a term I have seen in English fiction but itself not in dictionaries. <i>Summer sickness</i> has perhaps become less common with the ubiquity of refrigeration.I recall press references to it in the 50s and 60s.  It is also more medically diagnosed these days - e.g. it is attributed to salmonella or campylobacter or even giardia. It has been associated with the collection of rainwater from house roofs - that can be contaminated by bird droppings.]

>  .. our usually filled to overflowing Chemistry 1 lecture had only about 20 students present. On enquiring why, my New Zealand friend said in a hushed, embarrassed voice that it was "summer sickness". adding that the citizens of Auckland were laid low every year with this. I asked her what summer sickness was, and she quietly told me it was vomiting and "the runs". <i>(Sep 13, 2008,Listener (New Zealand Listener),5</i>)

>  <b>Barbara Anderson</b> And some Spanish cream, which she had read somewhere was an excellent culture medium for the summer-sickness bug if left unrefrigerated. <i>(1992,Portrait of the Artist's Wife,42</i>)

>  <b>Phyllis Davis in letter to husband Geoff</b> We are still putting up with Pupuke [Lake] water in the taps in spite of all the agitation some months ago and there is still the business of fetching fresh water from the tanks. Which reminds me there has been a tremendous amount of summer sickness in Auckland and most families have suffered ... <i>(Apr 11, 1941,Personal Communication</i>)

>  "If we got the summer sickness, instead of drinking lemonade, we always had L&P." <i>(Feb 24, 2007,Press, The,D2</i>)

>  .. Professor L.H. Briggs, associate professor of chemistry at Auckland University College, has spent 30 years studying the properties of these plants .. Koromiko, for instance, has been used to cure summer sickness ... <i>(Oct 12, 1955,NZ Herald,2</i>)

>  <b>Phyllis Davis in letter to husband Geoff</b> I believe I had a slight attack of summer sickness as it is politely called here. I see in the paper that it is very widespread in Auckland. <i>(Mar 30, 1941,Personal Communication</i>)

### summer spinach

CTN, p. 183 <i>Tetragonia expansa </i> summer spinach -->[?is this Andersen] Among the useful plants to which we are indebted to New Zealand, we must not forget their summer spinach (T. expansa), which was discovered in Cook's first voyage by Sir Joseph Banks, and `was boiled and eaten as greens' by the crew. It was afterwards seen by Forster at Tangataboo, though it was not used by the natives; but Thunberg found the Japanese aquainted with its value as a pot-herb. It was introduced into Kew Gardens in 1772; but the first account of it as a vegetable worthy of cultivation was published ... in the Annales d'Agriculture for 1809. <i>noun</i>.

[NOTES: Jim writes : NSOD defines this as a cork etc helmet formerly worn by whites in the tropics. Macquarie 1981 is similar., (Not in Collins). But I recall it from the 30s (and later?) as the name for a child's cloth sunhat made with an extension at the back to protect the neck. I have found no citations, however. DEH adds: I remember these. I think they disappeared when troops returned from the Middle East and the cult of protection from the sun gave way to the cult of the sun. ### sundowner

 
<i>noun</i>. formerly, a swagger who arrived at a place at sunset so that he could claim traditional food and shelter without the need to work for it.



 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a swagger or itinerant who arrives at a property in the evening when work is finished, hoping for a bed.

>  They are delighted to see the "sundowner" again; to see the "swagger" on the roads. <i>(1909,NZ Parliamentary Debates,146/102</i>)

>  Only let him occupy one of the many roadside farms to which he alludes for a few months, and be subjected to the daily and hourly pesterings to which we are subjected by hundreds of swagmen, sundowners, and other loafers - the majority of whom cannot do a day's work when they get the chance - and it strikes me very forcibly that his goodly Samaritan learnings [sic] would receive such a shock that he would experience no difficulty in understanding the reception he met with. <i>(Feb 22, 1871,Bruce Herald,6</i>)

>  <b>WILSON</b> .. they were odd members of the idle class known as the swaggers and sundowners. <i>(1894,In the Land of the Tui,248</i>)

>  <b>LOUGHNAN</b> sundowner: (ii): a swagger who times his arrival just at the right time for the evening meal. <i>(1981,Loughnan Glossary,81</i>)

>  The moon was shining brightly as the three "sundowners" approached. <i>(Feb 12, 1887,Auckland Weekly News,8</i>)

>  <b>BRADSHAW</b> The [peripatetic labourers] in the colony are known by the name of `Swaggers' or `Sundowners' Swaggers, because they carry a swag or bundle on their backs ... Sundowners, because they never approach a habitable place before sundown lest they should be requested to take a further stroll. <i>(1883,New Zealand As It Is,26</i>)

>  Old sun-downers told ... yarns of ferocious mastiffs ... It was quite certain that the most persistent swagger had never obtained the inevitable feed and shake down there. <i>(1889,Zealandia,1/31</i>)

>  <b>DAVIDSON</b> Kelly [a detective] had on more than one ocasion swagged it for weary miles after his prey as an orthodox sundowner, or in taking his turn in the harvest field, or at a threshing mill. <i>(1889,Stories of NZ Life,2</i>)

>  <b>WILSON</b> About these wayfarers Mr. Cameron had something to tell me, for they were odd members of the idle class known as swaggers and sundowners ... [249] So far as I could discriminate, swaggers (those who, snail-like, carry their worldly possessions on their backs) are men occasionally willing to do a day's work for a night's lodging and a couple of meals. Sundowners (those who have no possessions to carry) walk from station to station during the day, and, sleeping under a haystack until sunset, make their appearance at that hour before the `whares' or huts provided for them, and demand from the owners supper and shelter, which are generally granted. <i>(1894,In the Land of the Tui,248, 249</i>) [NOTES: 1891 Dec 21 in 1894 Land of the Tui]

>  <b>MORRIS</b> a tramp who takes care to arrive at a station at sundown, so that he shall be provided with <i>tucker',/I>(q.v.) at the squatter's cost: one of those who go about the country seeking work and devoutly hoping they may not find it. <i>(1898,Austral English,444</i>)

>  Possibly before next harvest we shall hear a cry raised by the squatter.. that those who are about do not want work; that they are sundowners. <i>(Mar 20, 1890,Otago Witness,15</i>)

>  <b>BRADSHAW</b> fn The term `swagger' is applied to a man who tramps from place to place in quest of work, carrying all his worldly goods in a swag, or bundle, thrown across his back. The `sun-downer' is one who tramps from place to place pretending to seek employment, but, as a matter of fact living upon the supper and breakfast with which he is supplied at most up-country stations. He fears to arrive too early in the day, lest he should be requested to seek a bed elsewhere, and hence the name with which he has been endowed. <i>(1888,New Zealand Of Today,181</i>)

>  <b>PYKE</b> Now, a `sundowner' or `tussocker' for the terms are synonymous - is a pastoral loafer; one who loiters about till dusk, and then makes for the nearest station or hut, to beg for shelter and food. <i>(1873,Wild Will Enderby,Bk III ch x 105</i>) [NOTES: (1889)]

>  <b>D'AVIGDOR</b> Those who join it [the professional unemployed] are distinguished from `sundowners' ... by working chiefly in towns instead of in the open country, and in swarms instead of alone. It has, therefore, several advantages over `sundowning'. The professional unemployed need not tramp ten, twelve, or twenty miles a day, and he always has congenial company. <i>(1888,Antipodean Notes,154</i>)

>  <b>D'AVIGDOR</b> The language of the Australian Colonies is not in the least like the last mentioned [`Daily telagraphese']. <i>(1888,Antipodean Notes,165</i>) [NOTES: [check spg???]]

### supervision

 
<i>noun</i>. a sentence introduced by the Criminal Justice Act 1985 to replace release on probation.

[NOTES: Jim Cameron writes : It subjects the offender to the oversight and control of a probation officer. <i>Supervision</i> in England is primarily a welfare order placing a child under local authority or probation officer supervision, although it may also be an adjunct to a suspended sentence. Note that the term <i>probation order</i> is no longer used in NZ, but <i>probation officer</i> is, and that <i>pre-sentence report</i> corresponds to the English <i>social inquiry report</i>.]

>  An extension of the leases would encourage the tenants to surface sow thier land, and, in the event of further severe weather, they could then save their sheep by hay feeding. <i>(Sep 7, 1904,Otago Witness,8</i>)

>  ..  a large portion of which a fire has run; having been surface-sown with grass. <i>(1902,Settler's Handbook of NZ, The,2</i>)

>  You do not state whether you require grass land for sheep or cattle, whether the seed is to be surface-sown or after the plough. <i>(Mar 1907,NZ Farmer,207</i>)

>  It is intended to surface-sow with grass-seed (principally Chewing's fescue, clovers, cocksfoot and crested dogstail) a block of mountainous country ... <i>(Sep 15, 1913,NZ Journal of Agriculture,343</i>)

>  Several courses were open to us:- (1.) to burn the existing growth, and surface-sow with a mixture of grass-seeds. <i>(May 20, 1921,NZ Journal of Agriculture,260</i>)

>  <b>STUDHOLME</b> Grass was surface-sown on the burnt patches ... <i>(1940,Te Waimate,101</i>)

>  Following the initial drainage work, the earlier farmers, after cutting down the remaining bush and scrub, burned off and surface sowed the land. <i>(Jan 15, 1945,NZ Journal of Agriculture,11</i>)

>  <b>ELLISON</b> Allison had broken in part of his and also had burnt and surface-sown some hills ... [surface sow] <i>(1956,Whirinaki Valley, The,38</i>)

### surface-sowing

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] the sowing of pasture grass seeds on the surface of the soil, without tilling.

>  By far too little attention is paid to surface-sowing of grass seed by those who have stretches of land in the native state. <i>(Mar 5, 1896,Otago Witness,5</i>)

>  His main improvement has been cutting down tea-tree on the better land, burning off, and surface-sowing: and he now has 120 acres down in turnips. <i>(Jan 30, 1913,Evening Post,11</i>)

>  <b>JOHNSTON</b> Rode out to run and looked at surface sowing. <i>(Apr 1, 1874,Johnston Diary</i>)

>  A little surface sowing with European grasses sometimes takes place after the spring burn. <i>(Jun 15, 1910,NZ Journal of Agriculture,8</i>)

>  .. districts which were either firstly infested with blackberry or Californian thistle; or secondly, bush-districts where the surface-sowing of grass-seed was the customary method of laying down grass. <i>(May 22, 1914,Hawke's Bay Herald,3</i>)

>  What grasses are best adapted for surface-sowing on this class of country, bearing in mind the dryness of the summer months? <i>(May 20, 1921,NZ Journal of Agriculture,313</i>)

>  Pastures were slowly established by felling the bush in winter and spring, burning the fallen timber and underscrub in the summer, and surface sowing English grasses and clovers on the ash of the burns. <i>(Apr 16, 1945,NZ Journal of Agriculture,346</i>)

>  <b>TAIT</b> By underscrubbing, burning off and surface sowing of seed, a beginning was made in the grim struggle of developing the land into a farm. <i>(1958,Farms & Stations of NZ Vol III,123</i>)

>  On the other side similar country is being developed by surface sowing, fertiliser and stocking. [surface sowing] <i>(Aug 13, 1970,NZ Farmer,51</i>)

### surface-sown

 
<i>adjective</i>. [Rural] [of land] sown in seed without tillage.

### surfer

 
<i>noun</i>. a surfacer q.v.

>  <b>VON HAAST</b> Generally the greater portion of the sand is removed, but in favourable spots, sheltered either by a slight indentation in the coast-line, or by some large pieces of drifted timber, its heavier particles remain; these consist [529] of black iron-sand (both magnetic and titaniferous oxide of iron) associated with small garnets and with gold. These black layers are often one or two inches thick, and repose upon coarse quartzose sands. As soon as a storm has subsided, the `beachers' or `surfers' as they are called, examine the coastline near their houses. When they come upon one of the rich spots, the fine particles of gold being often visible to the naked eye, they at once remove the black layer of sand out of the reach of the tide, and wash it when convenient. <i>(1948,Life & Times of Sir Julius von Haast,528-529</i>) [NOTES: 1868 Von Haast in 1948 Von Haast Julius Von Haast]

### swag

 
<i>noun</i>. a load, often as a bundle

<i>verb</i>. to carry as or in a swag

<i>verb</i>. [Rural] to travel on foot, carrying a swag.

### swing gate

 
<i>noun</i>. [Rural] a double-hinged gate used in a drafting race, to swing in two directions.

>  As the race has to be wide enough in all cases to admit of the passage of a large full-fleeced sheep, it often happens, in yards constructed on the old plan, that two small sheep get jammed and block up the way; but this becomes an impossibility upon Mr Sutherland's plan, as the sheep next the rollers easily draws a-head of the one next the rails, and therefore comes to the swing gate first. <i>(Jul 24, 1869,Otago Witness,14</i>)

>  <b>ELWELL</b> This was something like a 'race' for drafting sheep, with a swing gate. <i>(1878,Boy Colonists,214</i>)

>  The swing gate was the most valuable invention ever applied to the rapid and correct working of sheep. <i>(Oct 1885,NZ Farmer,293</i>)

>  <b>MOWAT</b> Made a swing-gate for sheepyards. <i>(Dec 18, 1906,Alexander Mowat Diaries</i>)

>  <b>PERRY</b> The draining pen will be divided in two having a swing gate at the gangway end. <i>(1922,Sheep Farming in NZ,23</i>)

>  <b>MARTIN</b> At the same time that fencing was becoming widespread, the swing gate was introduced for drafting. <i>(1990,Forgotten Worker, The,56</i>)

>  <b>POLACK</b> Among the piscivorous tribes, are those well known in Europe under the appellations of snapper, tench, haddocks, pollock, salmon, gurnets, john dory, hakes, bream, sword-fish, elephant-fish, diodons, pipe-fish, cod, parrot-fish, flounders, skate, cat and dog-fish, sting-rays, eels. - Among the larger tribes that sport in shoals in the vicinity of the shore, are, sperm-whales, called <i>para</i>[as-acute]<i> paraua</i>[a3-acute] (physeter macrocephalus); black whale, <i>mungu nui</i> (black physeter); right whale,<i> tohora</i> (balaena mysticetus); finback, (balaena physalis); sun-fish (diodon mola); large-lipped whale (balaena mysticetus); large-lipped whale (balaena musculus); hump-back (balaena gibbosa); shark, <i>mango</i> (squalus); hammer-head (zygaena); pilots, (scomber); flying-fish (exocaetus volitans); and an infinity of others, besides a great variety of testaceous and crustaceous fishes that almost cover the rocks under water, such as clams, muscles, oysters, crays, cuttles, limpets, wilks, gigantic muscles, a foot in length, cockles, sea-ears, sea-eggs, star-fish, mutton-fish, &c.; from the latter the pearl is procured which they insert in the eyes of their carved images and boxes. <i>(1840,Manners & Customs of the NZers,1/202 fn</i>)
